en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Unprecedented True Dharma,
Scroll One. Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Imperially Appointed Grand Officer of the Court of State Ceremonial, Acting Minister of the Court of State Guest,
and Great Master of the Propagation of the Teaching, the Subject Fata, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, there were eighty-four thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had gathered from various buddha-fields. These bodhisattvas all possessed great wisdom, had attained the great dhāraṇīs, were endowed with unimpeded eloquence, and had all realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). They entered samādhi and the gates of dhāraṇī-wisdom; they understood the inclinations and desires of all sentient beings, skillfully expounded the essential points of the Dharma, and were liberated in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, along with Śakra-devānām-indra, Mahābrahmā the Lord of the Sahā World, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, all came to assemble.
At that time, there was a great bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, who was on the side of that mountain together with a retinue of twenty-five great bodhisattvas. Their names were:
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nāgaśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nāgadatta, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śrījanman, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śrīgarbha, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Uttamalocana-śrī.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Padmaśrījanman, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Lokadhara,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dharaṇīdhara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnamudrāpāṇi, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhamati.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntaghoṣa, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gaganagañja,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samacittadharmacakrapravartin, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvapadārthaviniścayamahāpratibhāna,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Pratibhānasaṃbhava, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sāgaramati.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sa, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva King of Mount Sumeru, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Loving View, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Joyful King,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Boundless Vision, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Boundless Action,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Destroyer of All Māras, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bestower of Freedom from Sorrow.
the Mahāsattva Sarvārthasiddha Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Furthermore, there were four devaputras from Tuṣita, whose names were:
Samantamukhapuṣpa Devaputra, Prabhāsamukhapuṣpa Devaputra, Māndāravagandha Devaputra, and Vīryadharmacārin Devaputra.
Out of faith and joy, these devaputras each came with their retinues to the place where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was, in order to listen to and receive the True Dharma.
When the great bodhisattvas and the assembly of devaputras had arrived at the gathering, they sat down in order.
At that time, the great assembly all spoke these words:
"The Buddha’s omniscience is profoundly deep and immeasurable, vast and boundless, inconceivable, peerless, supreme and unsurpassed, and beyond full comprehension."
"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva don the armor of diligence and yet proceed toward the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
At that time, there was a great bodhisattva in the assembly named Nāgaśrī, who addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:

"If a bodhisattva plants various roots of goodness with a mind free from attachment and dedicates them to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), this is called abiding in the dharma of all roots of goodness while donning the armor of diligence; such a bodhisattva mahāsattva is then able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience."
The Bodhisattva Nāgadatta said:

“If a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of equanimity, a mind of subduing, a mind of affection, a mind of joy, a mind of pliancy, and a mind free from discrimination, this is called being firmly armored with diligence; such a one is then able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.”
The Bodhisattva Śrījanman said:

"If there is a bodhisattva who, throughout many eons, desires to fully comprehend the all-knowledge of a Buddha, they should don the armor of diligence for immeasurable eons, performing difficult and painful practices for the sake of all sentient beings without self-exaltation; such a one is able to advance toward the realization of a Buddha’s all-knowledge."
The Bodhisattva Śrīgarbha said:

“If bodhisattvas give rise to the mind that benefits others, do not cling to their own pleasure, and do not delight in meditative concentration, but are instead able to universally bring great benefit to all, dedicating immeasurable roots of goodness toward all sentient beings, they are able to advance toward the realization of a Buddha’s omniscience.”
The Bodhisattva Supreme Lotus Auspiciousness said:
“As the Buddha has taught:

if bodhisattvas, regarding all phenomena, perceive neither self nor other, neither the manifest nor the hidden, and are universally able to subdue them; being free from all arising and activity, they are fully capable of practicing all modes of conduct—this is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the dharma associated with śamatha.”
"Once one is able to practice it oneself, one can further teach others; such a bodhisattva is then able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Bodhisattva Padmaśrījanman said:
"If bodhisattvas are attached to worldly dharmas, they will be unable to fully comprehend the Buddha’s omniscience."

If one has no attachment to worldly dharmas, and is without gain or loss, without disrepute or fame, without praise or blame, and without suffering or pleasure, then there is neither increase nor decrease regarding all dharmas; this is called the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of the world, by which one is able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara said:

"If bodhisattvas benefit all sentient beings through various supreme practices and thereby achieve their own self-benefit, yet do not give rise to discrimination between self and others, but instead dedicate their roots of goodness to all, exerting great diligence and constantly planting various roots of goodness for the sake of sentient beings—this is called the bodhisattva’s establishment in supreme practices, by which they are able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience."
The Bodhisattva Earth-Holder said:

"It is like the great earth, which can produce trees, various medicinal herbs, and the like; it causes them to flourish and bear fruit until they are fully perfected, such that all things exist because of the earth."
Yet that great earth does not form this thought:

"I produce grasses and trees and bring them to maturity; I serve as the support upon which the myriad things abide; and all sentient beings grow and develop by relying on me, the ground of the dharma-realm."
He does not form the thought:
"I am able to produce sentient beings.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he gives rise to a mind of equanimity like the great earth, benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings for a long time, yet he does not form such a thought:
"I am able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
By abandoning such discrimination, one can immediately proceed toward the realization of the Buddha's omniscience.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi.
"The armor of diligence consists of practicing all supreme conducts, which are vast and immeasurable; one who does not possess great roots of goodness cannot practice them.

If Bodhisattvas abide in a mind of equanimity, free from discriminatory thoughts, such that they do not give rise to joy or anger toward sentient beings even in their dreams, and cause all beings to don the armor of the Mahāyāna and proceed toward the realization of Buddha-wisdom, abiding in equality without the intent of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—such Bodhisattvas are then able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience."
The Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta said: “May all beings in every realm of sentient beings be individually inspired to give rise to great compassion and universally bestow the Dharma-seal.

For those among these beings who lack faith, may they develop right faith; for those who have not heard the teachings, may they become widely learned; for those who are stingy and greedy, may they practice generosity; for those who violate the precepts, may they be complete in the foundations of morality; for those who harbor anger, may they practice patience; for those who are indolent, may they arouse diligence; for those who are distracted, may they abide in meditative concentration; and for those who are deluded, may they be endowed with wisdom. May they constantly cultivate wholesome dharmas, bringing them all to perfection and becoming fully possessed of roots of goodness.”
One should constantly practice the three kinds of precious seals of a bodhisattva. What are these three?
They are: causing the Buddha-wisdom of sentient beings to be perfected; and being able to dedicate all roots of goodness to all sentient beings—this is the first precious seal.
To universally benefit all through one's own performed virtues and to bring to fulfillment the roots of goodness in all sentient beings—this is the second jewel seal.
To contemplate the realm of sentient beings as being like space, pure by its very nature—this is called the third jewel seal.
"If a bodhisattva constantly practices these deeds without rest, they will be able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhamati said:

"If a bodhisattva is firm in their diligence and free from fear, such that they cannot be broken, possess no indolent mind, and have no thought of alarm or terror; if they are courageous and do not retreat, enduring toil and suffering within saṃsāra without cowardice or dread, and are thus able to transcend and realize nirvāṇa; if they abide in equanimity toward the phenomena of suffering and pleasure, without dualistic marks."
"One who acts in this manner is a bodhisattva donned in the armor of diligence, who is thus able to advance toward and realize the all-knowledge of a Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntaghoṣa said:
"For example, in the world, one who possesses great strength, who is difficult to bend or subdue, and who can accomplish whatever he undertakes, is called a true hero (satpuruṣa)."

As for such a true person (satpuruṣa), they constantly practice the True Dharma, remain free from all defilements of transgression, do not give rise to false views, and diligently perform great deeds; their minds are always supple, they lack coarse or evil traits, and they are free from all violence—this is called a true person.

One who constantly utters wholesome words, draws near to virtuous friends, honors teachers and elders with a sincere and respectful heart, and practices the right path in accordance with it without transgression—such a person is called a true gentleman (saddharmasatva).

Free from all craving and attachment, they practice the conduct of right livelihood; through pure karma they eliminate faults, and with a mind of wisdom they sever the views of ignorance. Abiding in tranquility regarding their own threefold actions, they do not disturb others, nor do they discuss what is good or evil, long or short; being without blame or praise, such a person is called a true gentleman (sajjana).

Out of compassion for the poor and destitute, he practices giving without distinguishing between enemy and kin; his inner mind is upright and his outward demeanor is gentle; he is free from all crookedness and maintains conduct of absolute truth; he delights his heart in the unsurpassed Dharma, remaining tranquil and steadfast, dwelling in equanimity—such a person is called a true gentleman (sajjana).

To destroy all obstacles for sentient beings; to be able to universally bestow one’s body, life, and wealth; to feel no difficulty or stinginess regarding the Dharma of ultimate truth; to eliminate all unwholesome dharmas for those sentient beings seen to lack merit and wisdom, and thereafter bestow upon them the treasure-trove of the sublime Dharma—constantly bestowing precious jewels upon impoverished and suffering beings, providing medicine to those who are ill, granting peace and happiness to those who are terrified, acting as a sovereign for those without a protector, delivering those fallen into saṃsāra, acting as light to illuminate and guide those in darkness, and showing the right path to those on wrong paths—always instructing all with the language of the Dharma, and not giving rise to anger even when seeing their faults: this is called a true gentleman (satpuruṣa).
"All Bodhisattvas should cultivate this practice; they will then be able to dwell securely in the dharmas associated with *śamatha* and proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"Bodhisattvas regard all sentient beings with impartiality, practicing the contemplation of great compassion as being like space, without limit or measure."
The practice of the contemplation of great compassion is likewise immeasurable and boundless.
One should constantly give rise to joy, guard the sense faculties, remain free from defiled attachment, and practice the dharma of the six pāramitās without weariness.
Practicing giving and the other perfections as being like space, without any obstruction;
observing morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom in the same way—the Bodhisattva is thus able to advance toward and realize the all-knowledge of a Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Equal-Mind-Turning-Dharma-Wheel said:

"If there is a bodhisattva who practices the path to enlightenment, they should not give rise to various signs or discriminative thoughts regarding any phenomena; thus, they will not be afflicted or harmed by Māra, will always be cherished and remembered by all Buddhas, will be constantly protected by devas, nāgas, and spirits, and the roots of goodness they cultivate will be genuine and without loss."

If a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind that perceives signs regarding phenomena and conceives discriminative thoughts, they immediately fall within the realm of Māra and are moved by Māra; such a one cannot be sustained by the Buddhas nor protected by the devas.
If one is firm and immovable, signless and non-conceptual, such a bodhisattva shall turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma for the sake of all beings. Why is this?

Because the Bodhisattva realizes that all phenomena are without arising and without activity, although the Bodhisattva gives rise to various states of mind, they remain without attachment; thus, by means of a signless mind, they realize the Buddha’s Bodhi.
This is likewise true even when turning the sublime wheel of Dharma.
"This is what is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva donning the armor of diligence, thereby being able to advance toward and realize the all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*) of a Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Great Eloquence Who Discerns All Phrases and Meanings said:
"Virtuous sirs, you should know that every place is bodhi."

Afflictions are bodhi; all conditioned activities are bodhi. Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are bodhi; unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are bodhi. Contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are bodhi; uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are bodhi. The mind of attachment is bodhi; the mind free from attachment is bodhi. Roots of goodness are bodhi; roots of non-goodness are bodhi. Mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*) are bodhi; supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*) are bodhi. Phenomena of saṃsāra are bodhi; the realm of nirvāṇa is bodhi. Falsehood is bodhi; truth is bodhi. The aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*) are bodhi; earth, water, fire, wind, and space are bodhi.

Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva understands that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty, all that they undertake is devoid of intrinsic nature; thus, they understand all meanings as they truly are.
Just as space pervades all places, so too does the dharma of bodhi pervade all places.

If a bodhisattva understands all dharmas, they shall possess eloquence and attain right wisdom to discern the meanings of phrases; thus, they will be able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa said:

"If a bodhisattva’s wisdom and liberation, as well as all that they do, are entirely ungraspable because the mind is signless (animitta), there is nothing to increase or decrease; it is unmoving and unshakable."
They understand all speech according to the principle of reality, such that neither slander nor praise can move them.
All the speech of non-Buddhists and all the speech of Tathāgatas—whether internal or external, whether hidden or manifest—are entirely equal and without distinction.
Knowing that all phenomena ultimately return to quiescence, the mind is free from attachment, stable and immovable, like Mount Sumeru, which possesses no characteristic of shifting or turning.
If a bodhisattva’s wisdom and liberation thus return to the mind of quiescence, they will be able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Bodhisattva Sāgaramati said:
“The great ocean of a bodhisattva’s wisdom is the destination of all phenomena, which are of one equal flavor.
Through extensive learning, the bodhisattva maintains the dhāraṇī of the nature of all phenomena, which is of one flavor and without distinction.”

One thoroughly understands that the fundamental, true nature of all phenomena is not non-existent; rather, phenomena arising from conditions are themselves the ultimate reality, from which all various roots of goodness are born.

One should know that these dharmas neither increase nor decrease; their fundamental and derivative nature is of inexhaustible benefit and merit, ultimately quiescent, neither annihilated nor eternal, to be known exactly as it truly is.

Furthermore, they give rise to immeasurable minds toward sentient beings, never forgetting or losing them; they constantly generate reverence and expound for them, impartially proclaiming the uncommon Dharma and extensively planting various roots of goodness for all sentient beings.
This bodhisattva is thus able to don the armor of diligence and advance toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Bodhisattva King of Mount Sumeru said:
“Virtuous sirs, you should know:”
The Buddha’s omniscience is not easily known; it is difficult to measure, so how could one possibly attain its realization? Why is this so?

If bodhisattvas can transcend the mental activities of all worldly beings, transcend the sights and sounds of all worldly beings, and even surpass all worldly beings in their faith, joy, and knowledge, and if they can produce a mass of merit from generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom that exceeds Mount Sumeru, then such bodhisattvas are able to attain the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Bodhisattva Loveliness-View said:
"A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates the objects of the six sense-fields as having nothing to be contemplated, even regarding conditions as having nothing to be conditioned. Why is this? "
Whether it be form or mind, they are pure by their very nature.
Because form is pure, the eye has nothing to behold;
because sound is pure, the ear has nothing to hear.
Because fragrance is pure, the nose has nothing to smell;
because flavor is pure, the tongue has nothing to discern;
because touch is pure, the body has nothing to perceive.
Because the dharmas are pure, the mind has no object of perception. Why is this?
Because the sense faculties are pure, being empty by their very nature.
There is no self and no other; there is no attachment and no aversion; their intrinsic nature is equal.
Contemplating all sentient beings, one sees that there is neither high nor low; they are all entirely equal.
One gives rise to a resolute mind regarding all Buddha-dharmas and does not harbor doubt or confusion.
One delights in the Dharma without weariness; having obtained it, one returns it as a gift, bestowing it without regret or stinginess, and is thus gradually able to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas.
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva acts in this way, they will be able to proceed toward and realize the all-knowledge of a Buddha.
Bodhisattva King Joy said,
"The bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells securely in a mind of generosity and forbearance."
If there should be someone who reviles, scolds, threatens, or strikes him, the Bodhisattva does not give rise to a mind of anger toward them, but instead conceives a thought of joy.
He constantly acts as a virtuous friend to all sentient beings, free from the notions of self and other, with neither one who can cause harm nor one who is harmed.

Since all phenomena are empty—both internally and externally—and because the marks of a self and the marks of a person are entirely empty, he constantly gives rise to a mind of joy and practices the giving of alms.
Should there be those who seek his head, eyes, hands, feet, wife, children, kinsmen, or even his very life, he gives them away with joy, without stinginess or regret.
A bodhisattva joyfully seeks the sublime Dharma; if they hear even a single verse, they would not be attached even to the rank of a Wheel-Turning King.
If they cause a single sentient being to resolve upon Bodhicitta, they would not take pleasure even in the rank of Śakra.
If they briefly hear a rare and wondrous teaching, they would not take pleasure even in the rank of Brahmā King.
If one is able to behold the Tathāgatas, even if the great trichiliocosm were filled with precious jewels, one would cast them aside as if they were mere shards of tile.

Delighting in the vision of the Buddhas, with joy perfected and the faculties complete, one will accomplish the factors conducive to enlightenment and be able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Bodhisattva Anantadarśin said:
"A Bodhisattva-mahāsattva is without the mark of self-view; observing that all dharmas are entirely pure, they give rise to no doubt or confusion, and are thus able to see all Buddhas."

He contemplates all forms without attachment and without the perception of form; he views all sentient beings without forming the notion of "sentient beings," and even his contemplation of all material images in the world is likewise so.

All Buddha-fields seen by the fleshly eye are entirely pure; because the retribution of karma is pure, one attains the perfection of the divine eye; possessing great supernormal powers, one attains the perfection of the wisdom eye; fulfilling the unique qualities of a Buddha, one attains the perfection of the Dharma eye; and being free from all afflictions, one attains the perfection of the Buddha eye.
"This bodhisattva shall attain the perfection of the ten powers and will be able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Bodhisattva Anantakārya said, "All that the Buddhas do is itself awakening."
Why is this? Enlightenment is that from which all-knowledge arises; it is born without internal thought, without external thought, and without anything in between.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva is without attachment toward any phenomena, they attain the complete extinction of the realm of afflictions without remainder; being free from demonic activities and having transcended the sphere of Māra, this bodhisattva is able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Bodhisattva Destroyer of All Māras said:
"If a bodhisattva does not give rise to the view of a self, they are immediately free from all views;
when no views arise, they can leave behind the activities of Māra and are thus able to fully realize the nature of the aggregates."
All aggregates are empty, and the mark of self is forever extinguished;
once the mark of self is extinguished, Māra can do nothing;
when the activities of Māra are extinguished, one is liberated from all obstacles.
"To be far removed from all hindrances is to attain Bodhi; this is called proceeding toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Bodhisattva Aśoka-datta said:
"If a person commits unwholesome karma, they will constantly give rise to anxiety and fear, repenting and reproaching themselves."
If one performs various wholesome deeds, there is nothing to fear or dread.

Therefore, a bodhisattva constantly practices wholesome dharmas without interruption, maintaining them in continuous manifestation; thus, they will not be harmed by the poisonous arrows of affliction and distress, but will instead don the armor of diligence and proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Bodhisattva Sarvārthasiddha said:
"If a son of good family is fully endowed with the dharma of precepts and fully endowed with practice and vows, he will be able to dwell securely in the root of the dharma of precepts."

For example, just as a sublime fragrance universally perfumes all things, so too can one leave behind all faults and distance oneself from all evils; only then can one fulfill the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), and once these factors of enlightenment are fulfilled, one achieves omniscience (sarvajñatā).
From this, one should know that the feet of ethical discipline are the foundation by which the factors of enlightenment are accomplished.
When a bodhisattva understands this, they are able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s all-encompassing wisdom.
When these bodhisattvas had each finished preaching the Dharma, there was among the assembly a devaputra from Tuṣita Heaven named Samantamukhapuṣpa, who spoke as follows:
"O Bodhisattvas!..."
For example, there may be a tree of exquisite flowers in the world that is in full and lush bloom, its color and fragrance fresh and beautiful, which many people love and delight in.
So too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: if their liberation from all phenomena is like the blossoming and adornment of flowers, they are loved and delighted in by all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

Furthermore, just as the trees growing in the gardens of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are vast, magnificent, and beautiful, with flowers blooming in exquisite abundance that are delightful and pleasing, so too,
when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is adorned by the blossoming of the liberation of the Dharma, they are loved and cherished by all Bodhisattvas, humans, and devas.
Just as the supreme great maṇi jewel is pure and free from blemish, possessing the power to fulfill all wishes,
so too the bodhisattva-mahāsattva has a pure inner mind, free from all defilements, and possesses the merit of the Dharma.
"In this way, one is able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha's all-encompassing wisdom.
The Devaputra Flower-Blossoming-Light said: "O Bodhisattvas!"
Just as the sun radiates light that can dispel all darkness, causing all forms and images to become manifest, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

possessing the light of wisdom and extending the torch of the sublime Dharma, they universally illumine sentient beings to eliminate the darkness of ignorance, making them all clearly perceive with penetrating clarity.
The light of wisdom shines forth, free from all darkness and gloom; one is no longer shrouded by ignorance and blindness, but constantly treads the path of radiance.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva leads and shows the way to all sentient beings who have lost their path, enabling them to practice the correct path and thereby attain the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
The Devaputra Manḍāravapuṣpagandha said: "O Bodhisattvas!
The exquisite fragrance of the maṇḍārava flowers is wafted afar, filling a hundred yojanas."

It is likewise for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who is endowed with precepts, concentration, and wisdom; the fragrance of their precepts, the fragrance of their concentration, and the fragrance of their wisdom pervade the world, being universally perceived by all.
If any sentient beings hear this fragrance, all their afflictions will be completely eliminated.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, being fully endowed with such fragrance of the merit of the Dharma, is able to advance toward and realize the all-knowledge of a Buddha.
The Devaputra Vīryadharmacara said:
"If Bodhisattvas become weary or retreat for even a moment, they will be unable to cultivate superior practices or attain the fruit of Buddhahood."

If one possesses a mind of diligence, not calculating the length of kalpas as a long duration but remaining courageous, planting various roots of goodness with a mind never weary or satisfied, and constantly practicing the eight kinds of factors conducive to enlightenment.
What are the eight? First, the method of encouraging and assisting practices that correspond to supreme conduct;
second, the method of constantly cultivating the four immeasurable practices of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Third, practicing the five kinds of supernormal knowledges and the methods of wisdom;
fourth, constantly practicing the four means of attraction—namely, giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation;
fifth, being fully endowed with the dharma of patience regarding the three gates of liberation.
Sixth, extensively proclaiming the sublime Dharma for others;
seventh, generating the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta;
eighth, employing skillful means to dedicate all merit toward the gathering of all true dharmas.
"When Bodhisattvas practice these eight dharmas, they are able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the assembly of Bodhisattvas and the host of devas, saying: "O Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas!"
When one is free from all conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena, one realizes the Buddha-wisdom.
How is one free from conceptual discrimination?
It means not discriminating the three realms, not discriminating various views, and not discriminating what is internal or what is... [external].
Externally, they do not discriminate between the stage of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, or the stage of the ordinary worldling;
nor do they discriminate between saṃsāra and afflictions, the subject that contemplates and the object contemplated, cause and effect,
the objective sphere and what is not the objective sphere, or increase and decrease.
"This is the view of self; this is the view of what belongs to self; this is stinginess and greed; this is giving; this is the breaking of precepts;
this is upholding the precepts; this is anger; this is patience; this is laziness; this is diligence; this is distraction;
this is meditative concentration; this is delusion; this is wisdom"—yet he does not [cling to these].
They do not differentiate between roots of goodness that can produce all wholesome dharmas and unwholesome roots that can produce all unwholesome dharmas;
they do not differentiate between worldly dharmas and supramundane dharmas, but abide in the dharma of equality;
they do not differentiate between the conditioned and the unconditioned, nor do they differentiate between having a mind of attachment and...
This is the mind of non-attachment, which does not discriminate between what is with outflows and what is without outflows.
Bodhisattvas should know that these dharmas are without discrimination; by abiding in the correspondence of equality, one is able to proceed toward the realization of the Buddha’s omniscience.
"Furthermore, O Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas!
The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas is fundamentally unobtainable. Why is this?
It is not an object of the mind, nor is it known by wisdom; only a Buddha realizes it.
Those who are equal to a Buddha are also equal in their omniscience.
Within omniscience, one contemplates that nothing exists.
Because there is nothing that exists, one has no attachment to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
It is not to be grasped as form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all ungraspable—this is called all-knowledge.
There is no mark of phenomena, nor is there any mark of non-phenomena; this is called omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

There is no perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) to be realized, no perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) to be realized, no perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) to be realized, no perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) to be realized, no perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) to be realized, and even the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) cannot be realized.
Why is this? Because all phenomena are unattainable.
Therefore, even omniscience is unattainable.
"Furthermore, O Bodhisattvas!
Omniscience cannot be apprehended within the three periods of time—it cannot be apprehended in the past, it cannot be apprehended in the present, and it cannot be apprehended in the future either."

Because it does not cling to the three periods of time, it is not an object observed by visual consciousness, nor is it an object observed by auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness. Why is this?
Because they are detached from all objective spheres. "O Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas!
Those who would achieve omniscience should abide in this manner."
Why is this? Because all phenomena abide in this same way. All phenomena are equal;
omniscience is also equal, and even the dharmas of the Buddhas and the dharmas of ordinary beings are entirely equal.
In this way, the equality of all dharmas is called omniscience.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide thus and should train thus.
For example, the four great elements are all devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); even their original inherent nature cannot be apprehended.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is empty.
All worldly phenomena, whether wholesome or unwholesome, are also unapprehendable because their intrinsic nature is empty.
Why is this? Because they are not subject to conceptual discrimination.
"Since conceptualization is empty, this is the true meaning.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī spoke these teachings, two thousand devaputras in the assembly attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and twelve thousand devaputras resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
