At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Saṃbhārasamudgata addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"We should now go together to the presence of the Buddha and inquire as to how a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should abide."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, without rising from his seat within the assembly, withdrew his bodhisattva form and manifested the image of a Tathāgata—endowed with all the marks and signs of perfection, indistinguishable from Śākyamuni Buddha—and addressed the Bodhisattva Pratibhānakūṭa, saying:
"The Tathāgata is here; you should now question him."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Pratibhānasaṃbhava, not recognizing the manifested form, took him to be the Tathāgata himself; he approached the Buddha and asked:
“World-Honored One!
"How should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abide?
The emanated Buddha replied,
"As I have acted, so should a bodhisattva abide."
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa asked,
"How does the Buddha, the World-Honored One, abide?
The emanated Buddha replied:

“The Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not practice the dharmas of precept-keeping, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom; he is not attached to the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm; he does not perform bodily karma, does not initiate vocal karma, and does not give rise to mental karma.”
In this way, there is no activity in any place whatsoever.
Son of good family!
All activities are entirely like a magical transformation.
The Bodhisattva Pratibhānasaṃbhava asked,
"Is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, also a phantom-like manifestation?
The emanated Buddha replied:
"It is so, it is so. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should abide in this manner.
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, World-Honored One, that you too possess the characteristics of a magical transformation?
The manifested Buddha replied, "No."
"Good son! All dharmas have the characteristic of being illusory transformations.
Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa said:
"So it is, so it is. All phenomena are empty by nature; they are all illusory and conjured forms.
How then could our Buddha, the World-Honored One, also be an illusion?"
The transformation Buddha replied:
"Good son! Is it only this Buddha who possesses the characteristic of being an illusory transformation?"
"All Tathāgatas whatsoever have the characteristic of being illusory transformations.
Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa asked:
"Who is the one capable of performing these transformations?"
The emanated Buddha replied:

"One's own karma is pure; there is neither an agent who emanates nor an object that is emanated. Furthermore, there is no self, no person, no sentient being, no life-span, no individual, no consciousness, no *pudgala*, and no characteristics such as a Buddha or an ordinary being."
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should one train to attain bodhi?”
The emanated Buddha replied:
"All dharmas are without anything to be learned; a bodhisattva should train in this way.
All dharmas are without anything to be practiced; a bodhisattva should train in this way."
All dharmas are without fear; a bodhisattva should train in this way.
All dharmas are without doubt or confusion; a bodhisattva should train in this way. All dharmas are non-existent and without an object of perception;

they are without falsehood, without accumulation, without activity, and without letters; they are without arising and without cessation, without having existed previously and without existing now; they are not illusory transformations, nor are they material forms; they are not what is observed by wisdom, being free from all conceptualization. A bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this way.
One who trains in this way is said to train correctly; there is neither decrease nor increase.
One who trains in this way has nothing to abandon and no conceptual proliferation; there is nothing to delight in and nothing to loathe; there is no joy and no anger; there is no coming and no going.
If one trains in this way, it is called right training.
Therefore, son of good family!

If there are those who seek to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should know that there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa; no grasping and no relinquishing; no giving and no stinginess; no precepts and no transgression; no patience and no anger; no diligence and no laziness; no concentration and no distraction; no wisdom and no folly; neither a learner (*śaikṣa*) nor one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*); neither practicing nor not practicing; nothing to be attained and nothing to be realized; no awakening and no Buddha-dharma; no notion of a self, no notion of a person, no notion of a sentient being, no notion of a life-span, and no notion of a *pudgala*; no notion of phenomena (*dharma*) and no notion of non-phenomena; neither a notion of existence nor a notion of non-existence.
Why is this? All phenomena are like illusions and transformations; they are non-dual, without distinction, and devoid of the characteristic of movement or change.
All phenomena do not consist of forms that can be grasped as signs; the eye cannot perceive them.
All phenomena are without the characteristic of discrimination and are not objects known by the mind.
The nature of all phenomena is emptiness; there is no dharma to be practiced and no bodhi to be attained. "Therefore, good son!..."
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice in this way and train themselves in this way.

If there are good sons who, upon hearing this teaching, do not give rise to alarm or fear, and do not give rise to doubt or confusion, such persons will be able to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
"Furthermore, good son! For example, space cannot be harmed;
fire cannot burn it, wind cannot move it, water cannot drench it, and dust cannot defile it; smoke, clouds, thunder, and lightning cannot adhere to it—because space is without obstruction."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: his mind is without obstruction and is not moved or turned by any phenomena; he has neither craving nor aversion, and his mind is like space, such that the various Māras, including those of the aggregates, cannot move it.
This bodhisattva shall realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and will be able to universally bring about great benefit for all sentient beings without end.
At that time, having spoken this Dharma, the emanated Buddha vanished and did not appear again, and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī returned to his original form.
The Bodhisattva Pratibhānakūṭa then addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"From where has the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, come?"
"Teaching the Dharma appropriately, where do you go now?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Originally there was no coming, and now there is likewise no going."
He asked again:
"From where does the coming of that which has no coming come? He replied:
"I have come from such a place.
Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa said:
"As the Buddha has spoken:..."
"All Tathāgatas have the characteristic of being illusory transformations.
As for that which has the characteristic of being an illusory transformation, does it not come from anywhere and go nowhere? Mañjuśrī replied:
"So it is, so it is. Just as the characteristics of a conjured being have neither coming nor going, so it is with all dharmas and all sentient beings.
Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa asked again:
"What do all phenomena abide in?
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī replied,
"All phenomena abide in the manner of having no intrinsic nature."
He asked again:
"Furthermore, how do all sentient beings abide? He replied:
"The karmic retributions of all sentient beings likewise abide in this manner.
He asked again:
"What are the karmic retributions of all sentient beings?"
He replied: "All phenomena are without arising and without karmic retribution; all phenomena are equal, and they abide thus now.
He asked again:
"If there is no karmic retribution, what constitutes this 'this and that' karmic retribution? He replied:
"The actions performed as they were done, and the retributions received as they were experienced—this is what is meant by karmic retribution."
He asked again:
"If the nature of the retribution of sentient beings' karma is empty, and their birth is likewise so, how then can they experience it? He replied:
"Just as in the true Dharma there is no karma, no retribution, and no arising, being neither existent nor non-existent—this is what constitutes karmic retribution.
Yet, the karmic retribution of sentient beings is never extinguished and never lost; that the nature of one's own karma is empty is the ultimate truth."

When the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī preached this Dharma, the Venerable Śāriputra, Ānanda, and other śrāvakas within the assembly of Śākyamuni Buddha heard the sublime Dharma spoken by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī through the power of the Buddha.
At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:
“World-Honored One! How rare!
Those bodhisattvas each expound the profound Dharma through various skillful means; if there are any who hear it, who among them would not resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates and trains in all practices with a mind free from attachment, and proclaims the sublime Dharma with a mind free from indolence.”
Śāriputra! Just as it is with the conduct of a bodhisattva, so too are the karmic fruits they attain, the wisdom they possess, and the teachings they proclaim.
Your own conduct and training, Śāriputra, are all the practices of a śrāvaka, characterized by attachment to signs.
"The wisdom thus attained is also like this.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Prabhāvyūha who rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is called the practice of the śrāvaka? The Buddha said, "Good son!

The practitioner of the Śrāvaka vehicle imposes limitations upon the Dharma; unable to remain free from signs (*nimitta*) regarding their practice, they delight in departing from birth and death to realize Nirvāṇa. They feel aversion toward and abandon sentient beings, being incapable of delivering them; their wisdom is narrow and inferior, lacking a vast mind.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva regards the practices of the Śrāvakas as being like those who are ignorant and blind.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva’s mental activities are free from attachment and his wisdom is without obstruction, enabling him to extensively deliver sentient beings and bring benefit to the immeasurable.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Prabhūtaratna again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Will the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and those great beings not come to this assembly at this moment to preach the sublime Dharma?”
We wish to hear it. Why?
Because the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī has realized the profound Dharma and entered the gate of liberation; with unimpeded eloquence, he skillfully expounds the essential points of the teaching.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha immediately used his supernatural powers to awaken Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and cause him to attend the Dharma assembly.

Thereupon, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, together with twenty-five great bodhisattvas and a multitude of devas and humans, all arrived at the place where Śākyamuni Buddha was. Each bowed their head at the Buddha’s feet in prostration, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Prabhāketu addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"How is it, Great Being, that you have departed from the presence of the Buddha to preach the Dharma in another place?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "The Dharma taught by the Buddha is profoundly deep and difficult to understand; it transcends all language and is not something that I can know.
Then, the Bodhisattva Prabhāvyūha said:
“The Dharma taught by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand.
Even a Great Being such as this, whose wisdom is immeasurable, cannot yet fully comprehend it; how then could we possibly understand it?”
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“Only Buddhas and Buddhas fully penetrate this; those who are not Tathāgatas cannot believe or awaken to it.

Therefore, I shall now expound the Dharma as I have received it according to my capacity, speaking only in accordance with the Dharma. It neither departs from nor does it not depart from the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). To speak in such a manner is called ‘expounding the Dharma.’”

Regarding all languages, all conceptual proliferations, all names and marks, and all arising and ceasing—neither separate from them nor not separate from them—the equality of all phenomena is what is called "teaching the Dharma."

All dharmas have no self-characteristic and no other-characteristic; they have no characteristic of dharma, nor do they have the characteristic of non-dharma; they have neither the characteristic of saṃsāra nor the characteristic of nirvāṇa—this is called the teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
What you have said, Mañjuśrī, is the true teaching of the Dharma."

Why is this? All phenomena transcend words and transcend all conceptualizations; there is no great phenomenon and no small phenomenon. Having severed all discrimination, they are not what is observed or seen by a mind in samādhi; not a single phenomenon increases or decreases.
"To expound the Dharma in this manner is called 'understanding the Dharma,' and it is precisely what is called 'seeing the Buddha.
At that time, as Śākyamuni Buddha was preaching this Dharma, eight thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
There were two hundred sons of gods who had recently set their minds upon the Mahāyāna, and they thought to themselves:

"The Buddha-dharma is exceedingly profound, difficult to understand and difficult to know, and cannot be fully exhausted; we shall ultimately be unable to comprehend its deep meaning, practice the various supreme deeds, and proceed toward the realization of unsurpassed bodhi."
"It would be better to seek nirvana through the fruits of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha vehicles; there would certainly be no doubt about that.
Thereupon, they withdrew their minds from the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what the sons of the gods were thinking, addressed them, saying:
"You all must not give rise to a mind of indolence or fall away from the practice of the Mahāyāna; you should resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, remaining firm and without retreat."

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, desiring to deliver the various devaputras, immediately manifested the body of an elder, holding a bowl filled with various flavors of food and drink, and entered the Dharma assembly.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he offered the food he had brought to the World-Honored One. Then, prostrating with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, he spoke these words:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for me, will accept this food of mine.”
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted this food according to the elder’s wish.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The food received by the Buddha is without limit; it should pervade the entire Dharma-realm while remaining free from attachment. There is no giver and no receiver; all are entirely equal, and thus he receives the food in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, Śāriputra conceived a doubt in his mind:
"From where has this elder who provides food come?
Is he not a manifestation of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī performing the work of a Buddha?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the doubt in Śāriputra’s mind, addressed him, saying:
“Do not harbor such thoughts, Śāriputra; whether it be coming or going, the Buddha himself knows the proper time.”
At that time, the World-Honored One took the food he had received and cast his alms bowl onto the ground.
The bowl he cast went to each of the Buddha-fields in the worlds below where Buddhas were currently preaching the Dharma; the bowl arrived before each and every one of those Buddhas.
The disciples of the various Buddhas each asked,
"From where has this bowl come?
and all the Buddhas replied to them:
“In the world above, named Sahā, there is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, titled Śākyamuni, who is currently preaching the Dharma.
This bowl has come from there, for the purpose of teaching and transforming all bodhisattvas.”

The bowl passed downward through Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers; there was a world named Prabhā, where a Buddha named Prabhā-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently resides and teaches the Dharma, and the bowl remained suspended in the air before that Buddha.
At that time, after Śākyamuni Buddha had cast down this bowl, he addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "You, Śāriputra!
By means of your supernormal power, observe where the cast-down bowl is now and in what place it abides."

At that time, Śāriputra entered ten thousand samādhi-doors; within those concentrations, by means of his own power of wisdom and the Buddha’s supernormal powers, he surveyed these bowls throughout ten thousand buddha-fields, yet he did not see where they were staying.
Emerging from meditative concentration, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
According to what I have observed, I have traversed ten thousand buddha-fields and have not seen the place where this bowl resides."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana, you should employ your supernormal powers to observe where the bowl you have thrown has come to rest.”

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, immediately entered eight thousand samādhi-doors. Within those meditative states, by means of his own supernormal power, he thoroughly surveyed this bowl throughout eight thousand buddha-fields in the world-systems below, yet he did not see where it was located.
Having emerged from meditative concentration, he came before the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!
By means of my own supernormal power, I have traveled through eight thousand buddha-fields in the world below, yet I did not see the place where this bowl resides."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying:
"By means of your supernormal powers, you should observe where the bowl you have thrown is now located and in what place it remains."

Subhūti, receiving the Buddha’s sacred command, immediately entered twelve thousand samādhi-doors; within those concentrations, he traversed twelve thousand buddha-fields to observe this bowl everywhere, yet he did not see where it was staying.
Having emerged from concentration, he came before the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!
By means of my own supernormal power, I have traveled through twelve thousand buddha-fields to search everywhere for this bowl, yet I do not see where it resides."
In this way, the five hundred śrāvaka disciples each used their own supernatural powers and the strength of their divine eyes to search everywhere for this bowl, yet none were able to see it.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
"Virtuous One, you have received the prediction of a single lifetime remaining before you shall succeed to the seat of a Buddha."
"I only pray that you will now enter samādhi and observe where the bowl has gone, so as to demonstrate this to the great assembly.
Maitreya Bodhisattva said to Subhūti:
"Venerable One!"

Although I have received the prediction that I shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in one lifetime, I am still unable even to know the names of all the samādhi-gates of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, let alone enter into them through realization.
Only the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī is able to fully realize all of this; there is nothing in his deeds or conduct that he does not thoroughly master. Subhūti!
How could I possibly know the deeds performed by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas?
Therefore, my supernatural powers and wisdom have not yet reached those of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
Now, as for this bowl cast by the World-Honored One, only Mañjuśrī can know its location; from this point downward, none are able to know it.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

The merit and supreme excellence of that Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī are such that, apart from the Tathāgata himself, none can surpass him; it should be known that he is the one whom the World-Honored One has cast the bowl toward."

“I only pray that the World-Honored One will command the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī to retrieve the bowl by means of his great supernormal powers and attend this assembly, thereby performing the Buddha-work before the great multitude.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: “Mañjuśrī!”
"You know where this bowl should go and where it should remain.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, having received the Buddha’s words, thought to himself:
"Without rising from my seat, without leaving the assembly of the Buddha, and without concealing my body, I shall take this bowl and show it to the great multitude."
Having formed this thought, he immediately entered samādhi; within that concentration, he extended his right hand across the world-systems below, passing through each and every buddha-field.
Before each and every Buddha, his hands emitted a voice that spoke these words:
"I now pay homage to all the Buddhas. My teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, sends his greetings to the World-Honored One:
'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?'"

Having extended his greetings, his hand emitted hundreds of thousands of koṭis of light rays from each and every pore. Within each light ray were hundreds of thousands of lotuses, and upon each lotus sat a Tathāgata; each of these Tathāgatas individually praised Śākyamuni Buddha.

Each and every world shook in six ways, manifesting great radiance that illuminated the Buddha-fields everywhere; furthermore, banners, pennants, parasols, and various kinds of ornamental implements appeared, performing the work of the Buddha.

In this manner, each and every Buddha-field was likewise traversed; having crossed through seventy-two Ganges-sand numbers of Buddha-fields, he arrived at the presence of the Buddha King of Light, and the way his hand emitted sound to pay homage and inquire after his well-being was also exactly like this.

Again, he emitted hundreds of thousands of rays of light; within each ray were hundreds of thousands of lotus flowers, and upon each flower sat a Buddha. Each of these Buddhas individually praised Śākyamuni Tathāgata, their radiance intermingling and illuminating one another until they penetrated through immeasurable realms.
At that time, in the assembly of the Buddha Prabhāsarāja, there was a bodhisattva named Prabhāketu who rose from his seat, approached the Tathāgata Prabhāsarāja, and said to him:
"From where has this hand come?"
Manifesting such signs, they emitted this radiance; furthermore, within that light, such lotus flowers appeared, and upon each flower were Tathāgatas, each of whom praised Śākyamuni Buddha.
"What are these signs? We pray that the Buddha will proclaim and reveal them.
At that time, the Tathāgata King of Radiance addressed the Bodhisattva Banner of Light, saying:

"Seventy-two *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddha-fields away from here in the upward direction, there is a world named Sahā. There, the Buddha known as Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently dwells, teaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings."

In that place there was a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, endowed with great merit, clad in the inconceivable armor of diligence, possessing great power of wisdom, and having already reached the other shore.
This bodhisattva, without rising from his seat within the assembly of that Śākyamuni Buddha, extended his right hand and took the bowl.
It was for this reason that such a miraculous response occurred.

At that time, the Tathāgata King of Radiance emitted a great light from between his eyebrows, which universally illuminated seventy-two Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, extending upward to the Sahā world and shining with vast brilliance.

Furthermore, all sentient beings in this world who were touched by the light attained great bliss, like that of a wheel-turning monarch; all those practicing the bodhisattva path who were touched by the light attained their respective fruits and perfected their own practices; all the great bodhisattvas attained the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi* gate; and all those practicing the śrāvaka path attained the dharma-gate of the eight liberations.

The bodhisattvas in the buddha-field of that Buddha King of Radiance, receiving the light of the Tathāgata, were all able to see this Sahā world, where Śākyamuni Buddha was teaching the Dharma, surrounded by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and the assembly of śrāvakas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāketu, seeing the sentient beings of this Sahā world afflicted by the turbidity of karma, shed tears of compassion and addressed the Tathāgata Prabhāśrīrāja, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Relying on the Buddha’s radiance, I am able to see that Sahā world; yet this world is filled with impurity and filth, such that the great bodhisattvas born there are like vaidūrya jewels submerged in mud.
"What is the meaning of this?
At that time, the Tathāgata King of Radiance addressed the Bodhisattva Banner of Light, saying:
"O son of good family!"
Do not speak such words.

Though those who practice the bodhisattva path in this world may cultivate meditative concentration for ten kalpas, they do not equal the sentient beings of that Sahā world who, by giving rise to a single thought of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, are able to obtain immeasurable merit and eliminate all heavy obstacles of affliction.
Why is this? Because the sentient beings of the Sahā world are fierce and sharp-witted.
Therefore, the bodhisattvas are born therein for the sake of protecting the Buddha-dharma; you should not give way to sorrowful weeping now.
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas within the gathering of Śākyamuni Buddha, having been illuminated by the light, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason has this radiance appeared, which is able to shine everywhere and cause us to experience great joy, while causing all sentient beings to extinguish their afflictions?”
Śākyamuni Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "Good sons!

Seventy-two *gaṅgā*-sands of buddha-fields below this world, there is a world named Prabhāsa. There dwells a Buddha, a Tathāgata named Prabhāsarāja, an Arhat, a Samyak-saṃbuddha, who currently teaches the Dharma and transforms sentient beings."
That Buddha emitted a great radiance from between his eyebrows, illuminating this world.
At that time, the bodhisattvas again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to see that world of Radiance, the Buddha Radiant King, and all the bodhisattvas; I pray that the Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers, will enable me to behold them.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha manifested the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of his feet; from within those wheels, he emitted a great radiance that shone downward, illuminating seventy-two worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, reaching as far as the buddha-field of the Buddha Prabhāsarāja, where it spread with vast brilliance.

At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas, riding upon the Buddha’s radiance, all beheld that Buddha King of Radiance and his bodhisattvas, and were thereby able to attain the dharma-gate of the Samādhi of the Sublime High Lamp.
At that time, the light from each and every buddha-field in the direction below shone universally, so that these worlds could see one another with total clarity and without obstruction.

In this way, the assemblies of bodhisattvas from all the worlds below, including the buddha-field of the Buddha Light-King, were able to see the bodhisattvas of this Sahā world, and each was able to gaze upon and pay homage to them.
Just as the sunlight dispels the darkness, so too do all sentient beings come to see one another.
At that time, those bodhisattvas each gave rise to a mind of diligence and strove toward the great fruit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī extended his hand before the Tathāgata King of Radiance and remained suspended in mid-air.

As he was about to take the bowl, a multitude of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of great bodhisattvas from countless buddha-fields respectfully surrounded him. Following the bowl, they ascended to the Sahā world, while the auspicious signs and radiant lights all gradually faded away.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī placed his almsbowl in the air before Śākyamuni Buddha and remained suspended there.
Thereupon, emerging from samādhi, he rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Receiving the Buddha’s command, I have taken the bowl that was cast down from the world below and now place it in the air before the Buddha; I pray that the Buddha will accept it.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One accepted it in silence.

At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas from the Buddha-fields of the lower direction who had followed the bowl arrived before Śākyamuni Buddha; they all paid homage at his feet and each invoked the name of their respective Buddha, saying:
"A certain Buddha, Tathāgata, Samyaksaṃbuddha, inquires after the World-Honored One:
'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy? Is your physical strength at ease?'"
"Are you not weary from teaching and transforming sentient beings?
Having thus extended his respects, he withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“Listen attentively now; I shall explain for you the past conduct and original causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
At that time, Śāriputra received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

In the past, incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Anabhibhūdhvaja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; that Buddha’s world was named Indestructible.”
There was an assembly of eighty-four thousand śrāvakas and twelve thousand bodhisattvas; that Buddha taught the Dharma of the three vehicles to transform and guide sentient beings.
That Buddha also appeared in the evil world of the five turbidities and expounded the Dharma of the six pāramitās for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
“Śāriputra! At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Jñānarāja, who was wise, discerning, and skilled in expounding the essential points of the Dharma.
When it was time for his meal, this bhikṣu donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered a royal city called Vistīrṇa to beg for food in due order.”
Having obtained a full bowl of various delicacies, he was about to depart from that city.

At that time, there was the son of an elder in the city named Viśuddhabāhu, who was still in his mother’s womb; seeing that bhikṣu passing by carrying the bowl, he immediately went before the bhikṣu, desiring the food and drink within the bowl.

At that time, the bhikṣu saw that this youth’s roots of goodness were fully matured and that he was a great vessel for the Dharma; he immediately took a ball of *modaka* from his alms bowl and gave it to him.
Having received that food, the youth felt a heart of joy and followed the bhikṣu Jñānarāja to the presence of the Tathāgata Aparājitadhvaja.
Then that youth went before the Buddha and prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
The Bhikṣu Jñānarāja took the alms-food he had received and gave it to the youth, saying to him:
"Offer this food to the World-Honored One and the great assembly; by doing so, you shall obtain an immeasurable mass of merit."
At that time, the youth, following the words of the bhikṣu, immediately took up the food and added it to the World-Honored One’s bowl;
he did so until the food was no longer sufficient, after which he served the rest of the great assembly in succession.
The bodhisattvas and śrāvakas in this assembly all received the food and were completely satisfied, yet the food was still not exhausted.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"After the youth Viśuddhabāhu had made this offering, his heart was filled with great joy, and he spoke these verses before the Buddha:"
"I have offered inexhaustible food to the Buddha and the great assembly;
having now completed this offering, I shall undoubtedly obtain a mass of merit."
The food offered is inexhaustible, and the Buddha’s merit is inexhaustible;
now that I make this offering to the Buddha, I shall surely obtain inexhaustible blessings.
With this inexhaustible food, I make an offering to the World-Honored One.
"May all roots of goodness increase, continuing on without end.
Thus, by offering a single bowl of food for seven days to the Tathāgata and the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, the food remained undiminished through the Buddha’s majestic power.
At that time, the bhikṣu Jñānarāja said to the youth:
"Having made this offering, you should take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha; receive the Buddha’s precepts and uphold them for as long as you live."
At that time, the youth accepted the instruction of the bhikṣu and took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Having taken refuge, he immediately gave rise to sympathetic joy and resolved his mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the parents of Viśuddhabāhu sought out their son and arrived at the assembly of the Tathāgata Anabhibhūdhvaja.
Having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and stood to one side.
Upon seeing his parents, the youth Viśuddhabāhu felt great joy; he inquired after their well-being and, before them, spoke these verses:
"Welcome now, my parents! Buddhas are exceedingly rare to encounter.
I seek great enlightenment for the sake of all sentient beings."
One should contemplate the Buddha’s marks and signs, as his body radiates wondrous light;
those possessed of wisdom should seek the fruit of Bodhi.
I now seek to leave the household life; I pray that my parents will grant me permission.
"He takes no pleasure in worldly riches, for a Buddha is difficult to encounter.
At that time, his parents spoke this verse to their son:
"We grant you permission to leave the home life and proceed toward unsurpassed enlightenment."
"By reason of you, I too shall train in this manner.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"At that time, the youth Viśuddhabāhu received permission from his parents to go forth [into the religious life]."
At that time, his parents conceived deep faith and joy; they also left the household life, took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and received them with gladness and trust.

Furthermore, at that moment, five hundred people simultaneously gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they all took refuge in the Buddha and left the household life, and the Buddha accepted them all.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"You should know this now:
as for that bhikṣu Jñānarāja at that time, could he have been anyone else?"
"He is none other than the present Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
As for the youth Viśuddhabāhu, he is my own self, Śāriputra."
"In the past, when I was the son of a householder, it was because that Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī bestowed a bowl upon me that I was inspired to generate the mind of great bodhicitta.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

From my first generation of the great bodhicitta until the fulfillment of the fruit, my ten powers, fearlessnesses, all merits, and possession of inexhaustible wisdom have all been initiated and guided by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
Why is this? The resolve I have generated is like space; it has no boundaries.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All the immeasurable and innumerable Śākyamuni Buddhas of the same name throughout the ten directions have all awakened the bodhicitta in the presence of Mañjuśrī, just as I have done.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Regarding the Tathāgatas Tiṣya, Puṣya, Dīpaṃkara, and Śikhin of the past—such Buddhas as these, I have praised their names throughout immeasurable kalpas. These Tathāgatas likewise, like me, gave rise to the mind of enlightenment in the presence of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, attained perfect awakening, and turned the sublime wheel of Dharma."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All those who practice the bodhisattva path first dwell in the Tuṣita heaven, manifesting the signs of descending to be born into the world;
they are then born into a royal palace, and subsequently undergo various ascetic practices."
"Up until their sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), all this is due to the teaching and guidance of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. Śāriputra,
you should know that the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī is the mother of all bodhisattvas, for he gives birth to all bodhisattvas."
“Śāriputra! All that I have spoken is true; you should understand the causal conditions of the past in this way.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, all the buddha-fields of the ten directions manifested various jeweled canopies and came to make offerings to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. From within each canopy, a great radiance was emitted, illuminating the Sahā world extensively.
Furthermore, from within the canopy, a wondrous sound emerged, speaking these words:
"Just as Śākyamuni Buddha has taught, so it is; so it is. In the past, he first gave rise to the bodhicitta from that Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva."

At that time, within the assembly of Śākyamuni Buddha, there were two hundred devaputras who had previously regressed from the resolve for bodhicitta. Seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī manifesting such various and inconceivable wonders, and hearing the Buddha explain the causal origins of these events, they each thought to themselves:
"The unsurpassed Great Dharma of all Buddhas is difficult to hear, let alone to witness the merit of the Tathāgatas being such as this!"

I should now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, abandon this inferior mind, give rise to the unsurpassed resolve for great bodhicitta, and resolutely proceed toward the fruit of unsurpassed great bodhi.
Having formed this thought, he immediately gave rise to the firm resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and never again regressed.
The Sūtra on the Unprecedented True Dharma Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Two.
The Sūtra on the Unprecedented True Dharma Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmadeva, Court Attendant and Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
Great Master of the Propagation of the Teaching, under Imperial Edict. At that time,
the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha, again addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"You should now resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, cultivate the various practices of a bodhisattva, and should not take pleasure in or become attached to the fruit of a śrāvaka."
Why is this? Śāriputra,
because all sentient beings dwelling within saṃsāra do not give rise to fear, they have no means by which to attain liberation.

Therefore, all bodhisattvas should arouse great diligence to transform and deliver sentient beings through various means within saṃsāra, causing them to fear birth and death and emerge from the triple world.
If you take pleasure only in the fruit of a śrāvaka and are unable to give rise to the mind of great bodhi to rescue and deliver all sentient beings,

then all sentient beings who encounter a bodhisattva and are exhorted to arouse diligence will immediately attain liberation from birth and death, and they too will be able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Śāriputra! In a past age, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Guṇasampanna Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
In this Buddha’s assembly, there were a hundred koṭis of śrāvakas and eight thousand bodhisattvas; that Buddha’s lifespan was one hundred thousand years.
There were two śrāvakas who were the most eminent leaders:
the first was named Prādurbhūta-jñāna (Appearance of Wisdom), foremost in wisdom.
One was named Śīghravikrāntagāmin, foremost in supernatural powers.

At that time, the Tathāgata, endowed with all virtues, dressed in his robes and took up his bowl at the hour of eating; surrounded by the great assembly before and behind him, he entered a royal city called Gandharvasvara and went on his alms-round from house to house.

When the Buddha entered the city, the śrāvakas of wisdom took their places at the Buddha’s right side, and the śrāvakas of supernormal powers stood at his left. The remaining assembly of śrāvakas followed behind the Buddha, while the assembly of bodhisattvas led the way in front. Furthermore, the Great Brahmā King, Śakra Devendra, the Four World-Protecting Kings, and the hosts of devas surrounded the World-Honored One as he entered that royal city.
At that time, there were three boys in the city, adorned with various ornaments, who were playing together by the side of the road.

These three boys saw from afar the World-Honored One, whose physical marks were upright and majestic, whose awesome virtue was immeasurable, whose radiance shone brilliantly like a mountain of gold, and whose dignified appearance was as venerable as a great dragon king.
Having seen him, they were filled with joy and gave rise to a heart of reverence.
The eldest youth said:
"Do you all see this Buddha, the World-Honored One?"
He is the most honored and supreme among all sentient beings; his mass of merit is inexhaustible, and he is revered by all in both the heavens and the human realm.
Therefore, we should collectively make offerings to him, for we shall surely obtain a great fruit.
Having deliberated together, the eldest youth spoke this verse:
“This Buddha is the most honored among all assemblies; He is worthy of offerings from both heaven and earth.
We should extend our acts of worship to him, So that we may obtain great rewards that are not in vain.”
The other two youths spoke in verse:
“I have no incense or flowers for offering, nor do I possess various exquisite ritual implements;
I have only this entire life of mine, which I shall now sacrifice as an offering to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.”
At that time, the first youth immediately removed the exquisite pearl necklace he was wearing—worth hundreds of thousands of measures of gold—and addressed the two youths with this verse:
"I shall now offer this necklace To the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Honored One of Great Wisdom;
Having extended this offering, May I obtain the unsurpassed mass of supreme merit."
At that time, the other two youths, having seen this youth present his offering, also each removed the necklaces they were wearing and addressed one of the youths with these verses:
“I offer these necklaces as an act of worship To the Most Victorious, the Honored One of Perfect Awakening.
Having made this sincere offering with a devoted heart, I vow to seek the True Dharma of the Buddha.”
At that time, the first youth saw these two people and also offered them a necklace, saying to them:
"The merit and benefit you have created are immeasurable; what kind of fruit do you seek within the Buddha-dharma?"
The second youth said:
"I vow that in the future I shall become a disciple on the right side of the World-Honored One and attain the foremost wisdom.
The third youth said:
"I vow that in the future I shall become a disciple on the Buddha's left side and attain preeminence in supernatural powers.
After the two youths had each declared their vows, they asked the first youth:
"You have skillfully guided us; you are our good friend."
"What do you seek by making this offering?

He replied, "My aspiration is that I may attain the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and be endowed with all-knowledge. May I emit light that shines forth, causing all who see it to rejoice and resolve upon Bodhicitta, just like the Lion King surrounded by his great assembly, no different from the Buddha as he is today."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“When those three youths each made their respective vows, eight thousand devaputras in the sky simultaneously raised their voices, saying:
‘Excellent, excellent!’”
"You have spoken these words well; the excellent fruit you hope for is certain and beyond doubt.
Then the three youths, each holding a necklace, went before the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“The Tathāgata, endowed with all merits, saw the three youths bringing various necklaces and approaching the place where the Buddha was. He then said to the bhikṣu Sāgaramati: ‘Bhikṣu!’”
"Do you see these three youths?
Sāgaramati addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"Yes, indeed; I have seen it. The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"

The aspirations of the first youth differ from those of the second; his lifting and lowering of his feet is exceptionally sovereign and majestic—like that of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin), such that even hundreds of thousands of Brahmā kings or Śakras could not equal him. Having now come to the presence of the Buddha, he has awakened the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), desiring to attain and realize unsurpassed bodhi.

When these three youths had arrived at the place where the Buddha was, each bowed his head to the ground in prostration at the World-Honored One’s feet and offered their necklaces to the World-Honored One.
Once the Buddha had accepted them, those who had resolved for the mind of a śrāvaka found their offered necklaces remaining before the Buddha;

those who had resolved for bodhicitta found their offered necklaces remaining in the air above the Buddha, transforming into a four-pillared jeweled pavilion adorned on all four sides. Upon it sat immeasurable Buddhas in the full lotus posture, manifesting various marks and signs of excellence, with infinite and most sublime adornments.

At that time, the Tathāgata, endowed with all merits, entered into samādhi and universally observed the manifestations of the transformations of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas. From his face, he emitted rays of light of various colors—namely blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, and green. This radiance shone universally throughout boundless worlds, reaching upward as far as the Brahma Heaven, so that it eclipsed the light of the sun and moon until they were no longer visible.
Once the light had shone forth, it circled to the right three times and returned to enter the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.
At that time, the bhikṣu Sāgaramati came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"By what causes and conditions has this radiance been emitted?
I pray that the World-Honored One will reveal it to me so that I may know.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“Do you see these two necklaces offered by the two youths standing before the Buddha?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha,
“Indeed, I have seen them.”
The Buddha said, “Bhikṣus!
Because these two youths seek the fruit of a śrāvaka, they desire to realize the nirvāṇa that benefits themselves; they are unable to give rise to the mind of great bodhi.”
"O Bhikṣus!

Do you see how the necklace offered by the youth before you is performing various transformations in the air above the Buddha? This person does so because he desires to realize unsurpassed bodhi for the benefit of all sentient beings."
Those two youths delighted only in wisdom and supernatural powers, and were unable to universally bring benefit and happiness to others.
For this reason, the offerings they presented also lacked any mark of excellence.

You should know that the meritorious deeds performed by one who has resolved upon the great bodhicitta are likewise immeasurable; you should now abandon the mind of a śrāvaka and seek instead for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Was that youth who at that time resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind anyone else?
It was none other than myself."
He who delights in wisdom is none other than yourself; he who delights in supernormal powers is none other than Maudgalyāyana.

Although you disciples have escaped saṃsāra, you seek only to enter nirvāṇa, and thus are ultimately unable to extensively benefit sentient beings with minds equal to those of the Buddhas—vast as space, inexhaustible, possessing immeasurable accumulations of merit and immeasurable virtues, surpassing the realms of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
“Śāriputra! You all should quickly resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the great śrāvakas—Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, Upāli, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, and the rest—spoke with one voice and in unison as follows:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
You have skillfully provided guidance, causing us to give rise to the mind of great bodhi.
World-Honored One!”

It should be known that good sons and good daughters who plant various roots of goodness and seek liberation ought to give rise to a vast mind and vast vows of conduct; such persons shall behold hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and hear the true Dharma.
“World-Honored One!

Since time immemorial, our wisdom has been narrow and inferior, and we did not dare to aspire to the boundless wisdom of the Buddha. Now, we deeply reproach ourselves and shall resolve to give rise to the Great Mind.”

For example, if a person has committed various unwholesome deeds and does not repent their transgressions, nor reform their evil ways to follow the good, there is no way for them to escape suffering and affliction.
Likewise, we śrāvakas seek only our own benefit; if we do not abandon this inferior mindset and seek the wisdom of a Buddha, we will ultimately be unable to escape the nirvana without remainder.
Furthermore, just as the consciousness of one at the point of death becomes clouded and confused, such that they can no longer look back with affection upon their beloved kin and relatives;
so too it is for us: if we seek only our own benefit and nirvana, we likewise lack the intention to transform and deliver all sentient beings.
“World-Honored One!
You should know that Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is like the great earth; all sentient beings in the world dwell upon the earth and are born from the earth.
All roots of goodness depend upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi to grow and flourish; it should be understood in this same way.”

At that time, there were ten thousand people in the assembly who, having heard the Buddha’s account of past events and causes and conditions, and having heard these words spoken by Śāriputra, all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the King of Magadha, having prepared his carriage with solemnity, came to where the Buddha was.
Upon arriving at the assembly, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the king joined his palms toward the Buddha and, with single-minded reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason do all sentient beings create karma?"
“Upon what do the causes and conditions for creating karma depend?
The Buddha said, “Great King!”
All sentient beings, from those with a lifespan to individuals (*pudgala*), all abide in the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and engage in inverted conceptualization;
because of this conceptualization, they give rise to afflictions and create karma;
because they create karma, they do not attain liberation.
The King asked again:
"World-Honored One!
What is the root of my view of a self?"
The Buddha said:
"Ignorance is the root.
He asked again:
"What is the root of this ignorance?
The Buddha replied,
"Improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) is its root."
He asked again:
"What, furthermore, is the basis for improper mental attention?
The Buddha replied:
“An uneven mind is the root. He asked again:
“What is meant by an uneven mind?”
The Buddha said:
"To not know things as they truly are since beginningless time is called an unbalanced mind.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'not knowing things as they truly are'?
The Buddha said:
"That all sentient beings, from beginningless time, have conceived existence where there is no [self], is what is meant by not knowing things as they truly are."
He asked again:
"How can one conceive of existence within that which is non-existent?
The Buddha said:
“The dharmas of conceptual discrimination do not arise and are not real, yet they are reckoned as existing.
He asked again:
“If dharmas do not arise, what is it that you now speak of?”
The Buddha said:
"Great King! Even my body is empty; there is no dharma to be taught."
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
If the body is empty, what does it do?"
"In what does it abide?
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
"Although there is that which is performed, there is likewise no attachment.
He asked again:
"Regarding this very non-attachment, how should it be explained?"
The Buddha said:
“That which is the teaching of non-attachment, spoken in accordance with reality—this is what is spoken by the Noble Ones.
He asked again:
“What is called ‘speaking according to reality,’ and what is called ‘that which is spoken by the Noble Ones’?
The Buddha said:
“Great King! To be free from dust and free from views regarding all phenomena is true speech; this is called speaking according to reality.
Speaking according to reality is what is spoken by the Noble Ones.”
"What the Noble One has taught is this: that one should thoroughly understand that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; one should abide thus and train thus.
At that time, King Magadha, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, felt great joy in his heart and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare it is, World-Honored One!"
This Dharma has been well-expounded; it is truly unprecedented.

Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, out of his untainted wisdom, universally preaches the true Dharma for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, yet all sentient beings, being entangled by their own sinful karma, are unable to hear, receive, or practice it; so too am I.
The World-Honored One reflected:
"From the past until now, I have not encountered virtuous friends; with an unwholesome mind, I have also extensively committed various unwholesome karmas.
For this reason, I have been unable to draw near to the World-Honored One or hear the True Dharma."

Within my deep palace, I take pleasure only in amusements, food and drink, and feasting; day and night, I never for a moment grow weary of them or abandon them. Therefore, I am unable to go to the Buddha to hear the True Dharma.
World-Honored One!

I now repent and reproach myself for the evils I have committed in the past; reflecting deeply upon them, I find no leisure for peace or joy day or night, like a man burdened by guilt who is constantly filled with alarm and fear.

The World-Honored One, with great compassion, is the father of sentient beings: he acts as a protector for those without refuge, a guide for those without eyes, a source of peace and happiness for those afflicted by suffering, a revealer of the true path for those who have lost their way, and a bestower of precious jewels upon those who are destitute.
His mind is impartial and free from weariness; he is universally able to bring benefit and happiness, harboring no thoughts of enmity or favoritism.
World-Honored One!
I pray only that you will take pity on me and deliver me.
As I reflect upon the transgressions I have previously committed, I am truly filled with dread, like one on the verge of falling into a pit, longing only for deliverance.
Fearing that I shall fall into the evil realms, I pray that the Buddha will protect me, extinguish the defilement of my sins, and awaken me to the True Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the King of Magadha had repented for his past misdeeds, felt a profound sense of disclosure and remorse, and took great delight in the profound Dharma of the Mahāyāna, thought to himself:
"Only the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, with his wisdom and eloquence, is capable of expounding this."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power and knowing the Buddha’s thoughts, addressed the King of Magadha, saying:
“Great King, you should know:

the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī possesses immeasurable eloquence and immeasurable wisdom; he is skilled in expounding the essentials of the Dharma and will surely be able to proclaim the True Dharma for Your Majesty, causing you to attain understanding and obtain great peace and happiness.”
It is fitting that you extend your request to provide a meal offering within the royal palace; this will bring benefit to immeasurable beings.

Furthermore, it will cause all the people of Rājagṛha to gaze upon, pay homage to, and praise [the Buddha], and by seeing, hearing, and rejoicing, they shall plant various roots of goodness and obtain supreme merit.
At that time, the King of Magadha, following the words of the Venerable One, went before the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and said:
"O Bodhisattva of great compassion, out of pity for me, please accept my invitation to take a meal within my palace; I pray that you will graciously accept my request at this time."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī said to the king:
"I have accepted your invitation; it shall be according to your wish.
Since you have generated this supreme resolve and I have already accepted your offerings, I am eager to hear the Dharma and shall therefore proclaim it."
"Great King!
You should preach the Dharma for the king by being without attachment to any phenomena;
you should preach the Dharma for the king by having no thoughts of doubt regarding any phenomena."
He preached the Dharma for the king by not clinging to the marks of the three periods of time regarding all phenomena;
he preached the Dharma for the king by not regarding śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or nirvāṇa as the mark of quiescence regarding all phenomena.
The king addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Excellent! How rare! I pray that the Bodhisattva, out of compassion for me, will accept this offering together with the great assembly.”
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said: "Great King,
let us set this matter aside for now."
Just as when a king provides food, drink, and clothing for the great assembly out of compassion and offers them as a gift, this is likewise neither for the sake of profit nor for the sake of merit.

Now, as for making offerings: it is to give rise to a mind of rare aspiration toward the Dharma, free from the notions of agency, self, sentient beings, life-span, or persons (pudgala); it is to be unattached to the characteristics of self and unattached to the characteristics of others—this is what constitutes making offerings.

One should contemplate all phenomena as being without grasping, without aggregates, bases, or elements; neither internal nor external; not abiding within the three realms, yet not apart from the three realms; neither good nor evil; without desire or aversion; neither mundane nor supramundane; neither with outflows nor without outflows; neither conditioned nor unconditioned; neither possessing afflictions nor free from afflictions; neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
"If it be thus, this constitutes an offering.
The King spoke again to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:
"Out of compassion and for the sake of my benefit and happiness, I pray that you will accept this offering."
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said: “Great King!
You should not seek benefit or happiness, nor should you feel any compassion.”
This mind is without attachment; it is unmoving and non-rotating, without praise or blame, without grasping or abandoning.
Because it seeks neither profit nor pleasure and has no object of compassion, all phenomena are equal and nothing is attained; this is called receiving offerings.
"Great King!
If it is thus, this is true benefit and happiness.
The King addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"The Dharma is fundamentally without marks and without activity; my offering of worship should likewise be thus.
Mañjuśrī said: "Emptiness is without marks and without activity."
One who seeks the Dharma is without conceptualization, without aspiration, without mental formation, without volitional action, and yet is not without volitional action.
Why is this so? Great King!
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fundamentally unmoving and devoid of activity.
The intrinsic nature of sentient beings is fundamentally empty, and their three karmas have no action or movement.
Great King!
"One should contemplate that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely without action, because one realizes that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all dharmas is empty.
The King asked: "If conditioned phenomena involve volitional activity (*abhisamskāra*), how can they be called 'without'?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Great King!

Just as past phenomena have already ceased, future phenomena have not yet arrived, and present phenomena have no place of arising, so too it is with all conditioned formations (saṃskāra) and the conditioned (saṃskṛta)."
Therefore, one does not cling to the three periods of time because all things are impermanent; phenomena neither increase nor decrease.
Great King, you should understand all conditioned formations in this way.
The King asked,
"Are the noble path and afflictions two dharmas that are equal? Mañjuśrī replied:
"These two are equal, with neither increase nor decrease.
Great King,
when the sun rises, does it join with the darkness?"
The king said: "No.
When the sunlight emerges, all darkness is dispelled."
Mañjuśrī said: "When the sun rises, where do those various darknesses go?
The king replied:
"Furthermore, that darkness also does not go anywhere. Mañjuśrī said:
"Afflictions and the noble path are likewise so; these two do not depend upon one another, nor do they increase or decrease, and they neither abide nor do not abide."
"Great King!
Defilements are equal and the Noble Path is also equal; because these two are equal, all phenomena are equal.
Great King, you should know this:"
The nature of afflictions is empty and has no place of abiding.
It is because of afflictions that one attains the Noble Path;
because one attains the Noble Path, there are no further afflictions.
"Therefore, these two neither increase nor decrease, nor is there any distinction between them.
The King asked:
"From what do afflictions and the noble path arise?"
Mañjuśrī replied, “They arise from the mind.
If the mind does not arise, afflictions will no longer arise.”
When afflictions do not arise, the noble path does not arise again.
Therefore, one should know:
afflictions are to be viewed in this way, and the noble path is likewise to be viewed in this way.
Having observed in this way, the mind finds nothing to be attained.
The King asked:
“Does the Dharma of the Noble Path lead to Nirvana?”
Mañjuśrī replied: "No.
All phenomena have neither coming nor going; nirvāṇa is likewise."
The King asked,
"In what manner should the Noble Path abide? Mañjuśrī replied:
"The Noble Path abides in this way.
The King asked:
"Does the Noble Path not abide in that which is beyond precepts, concentration, and wisdom?"
Mañjuśrī said: “All phenomena are without activity and without marks, being free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
That which consists of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom is itself conceptual proliferation, involving activity and marks; one should not abide in such a way.”
"One who abides in this manner neither abides nor does not abide;
the Noble Path is likewise.
The King said:
“Do all sons and daughters of good family who practice the path to enlightenment attain the noble path?
The Bodhisattva replied,
“For one who practices for enlightenment, there is not the slightest dharma that can be attained.”

The path to enlightenment is neither suffering nor pleasure, neither self nor non-self, neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pure nor defiled; it is not a saṃsāra to be weary of, nor is it a nirvāṇa to be realized.
"Therefore, all phenomena are unattainable, and even the dharmas of the noble path are unattainable.
The King spoke again to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent, Great Being!"
This is most rare; you have skillfully expounded the essential points of the Dharma, and I have full faith and understanding in them.
Now, with sincere heart, I respectfully prepare offerings; I shall provide food and drink for the great assembly, and the Bodhisattva should now accept my invitation.
Mañjuśrī said: “The food is without action; the gift is without recipient.
The giver and the receiver are non-dual and without distinction.”
"Since the King’s heart is sincere, he shall receive the King’s offerings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Now is precisely the right time; accept the King’s invitation, for it will bring great benefit to many people."
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Having now received the holy command of the Buddha, I have accepted the King's invitation; I shall, together with the great assembly, receive his offerings."

At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, knowing that the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had accepted his invitation, felt great joy and attained profound peace and security; he then paid homage to the World-Honored One, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and the entire assembly.
Thereupon, he went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was and asked him,
"How many bodhisattvas will come together with the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī to receive my offerings?"
Śāriputra said, "I shall go to the royal assembly together with a multitude of five hundred great bodhisattvas.

At that time, the King of Magadha first returned to his palace and adorned a vast hall. He commanded all his attendants to purify their minds and prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink. He arranged banners and precious, wonderful canopies, scattered various beautiful flowers, and burned diverse incenses. With pearls and necklaces of the utmost splendor, he laid out five hundred seats.
Furthermore, they had the roads within the royal city strictly repaired, scattering flowers and burning incense so that there was no dust or filth, making the way pure and solemn.

At that time, when the people of the city heard that the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was proceeding to the royal palace to receive the King’s offerings, they all felt great joy; with single-minded longing and veneration, each took fragrant flowers and waited by the roadside.
At that time, during the first watch of the night, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī reflected thus:

"I shall attend the King’s invitation tomorrow morning; however, the assembly of Bodhisattvas who will go with me is small. I should now go to various Buddha-fields to invite a great multitude of Bodhisattvas to join us at the royal palace for this magnificent assembly."
"If I were to preach the Dharma for the sake of the king, those bodhisattvas would be able to act as witnesses.

Having thought this, he immediately vanished from his original location and, in a mere moment, passed through eighty thousand buddha-fields to the east, arriving at a world named Constant Sound (*Nitya-ghoṣā*). There dwelt a Buddha named Auspicious Sound Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who was currently preaching the Dharma, expounding the Mahāyāna teachings for various bodhisattvas; all those bodhisattvas were of the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
In that buddha-field there are trees made of the seven precious substances, which produce various flowers and fruits;

the branches and leaves of these trees constantly emit subtle and wondrous sounds—namely, the sound of praising the Buddha, the sound of praising the Dharma, and the sound of praising the bodhisattvas of the stage of non-retrogression. These sounds of the Three Jewels are constantly produced, and thus it is called the World of Constant Sound.
Once the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had arrived there, he approached the Tathāgata Śrīghoṣa, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:
"I have come here from the Sahā world specifically to accept an invitation from the King of Magadha for a meal and offerings within his palace."

Because the assembly of bodhisattvas is small, I have come to invite these great bodhisattvas, the superior beings, to attend with me tomorrow morning at the royal palace to receive his offerings, so that all those sentient beings may fully receive his merit.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will command the bodhisattvas to accept my invitation.
At that time, the Tathāgata Auspicious Sound addressed eighty thousand great bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of good family!"

Now the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī has come to invite you all to go to that Sahā world to attend a meal offering at the palace of the King of Magadha; you should now go there together to perform the work of the Buddha.
At that time, the bodhisattvas immediately set out to carry out the World-Honored One’s instructions.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī paid his respects and took leave of the Tathāgata Śubhasvara; accompanied by eighty thousand great bodhisattvas, he vanished from sight and returned to the Sahā world, arriving at his original dwelling place.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had taken his seat together with the various bodhisattvas, he addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"I possess a dharma-gate named Great Dhāraṇī; I shall now analyze and expound it for the sake of you great beings."
What is called the Dharma-gate of Dhāraṇī? It is this:

those who desire to joyfully seek realization of the Dharma-gate of Dhāraṇī should abide in right mindfulness with an undistracted mind, free from all delusion and anger, and attain penetrating wisdom regarding all phenomena.

Practicing the path of the Tathāgata, they attain the gateway of eloquence, abide in the signless, enter the gateway of the wisdom of the dhāraṇī of all phenomena, and by continuing the noble path, they are able to sustain the Triple Gem.

In whatever discourse they engage, there is no obstruction; they skillfully understand the languages of all sentient beings, and when faced with challenges or debates, they provide detailed analysis, remaining free from fear in the midst of the great assembly.

Regarding all the various distinctions in speech and sound—whether of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, up to Śakra and Brahmā, and down to the diverse classes of animals—he is able to preach the Dharma by means of each and every one of those various modes of speech.
They skillfully know the sharp or dull faculties of sentient beings, enabling each to attain understanding according to their kind.
Their faculties are pure, they are free from all false views, and they dwell in equanimity within the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī.
He does not cling to the eight worldly conditions of favor and adversity, but brings all supramundane wholesome dharmas to perfection.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he explains their karmic actions, causes, conditions, and retributions, enabling them to attain great peace and happiness.
With wisdom that penetrates all things, they are able to cause sentient beings to cast off their heavy burdens.
Their minds are free from sorrow and affliction as they know the self-nature of phenomena.
According to the faculties [of others], they expound the Dharma appropriate to their ailments, causing them to arouse diligence and attain all manner of wholesome benefits.
"The Bodhisattva’s mind gives rise to joy without hoping for karmic retribution; all roots of goodness are dedicated solely toward omniscience.
Seeking omniscience, he acts universally for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings."
They are fully capable of accomplishing all practices of the six perfections: they perfect the practice of giving and dedicate it to omniscience;
they perfect the practice of ethical discipline and dedicate it to sentient beings, causing them to dwell in peace and happiness;
they perfect the practice of patience and attain the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha, becoming fully adorned with them.
Perfected in diligence, they bring all roots of goodness to maturity;
perfected in meditative concentration, they attain the corresponding dharmas with sovereign mastery and unimpededness;
perfected in wisdom, they penetrate all phenomena—attaining sovereignty and remaining free from all faults.
“O sons of good family!
Such is this dharma-gate of dhāraṇī—having attained this dharma-gate, one forgets nothing, for it enables one to fully uphold all-knowledge.”
"Furthermore, noble son! This dharma-gate of dhāraṇī can also receive and uphold all dharmas, namely:

realizing that all dharmas are empty, signless, and wishless; unmoving and unconditioned; free from conceptual discrimination; neither arising nor ceasing; neither annihilated nor eternal; neither existent nor non-existent; neither coming nor going; neither formed nor destroyed; neither aggregated nor dispersed; neither having a nature nor lacking a nature; neither having perception nor lacking perception; free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); and being without self, person, sentient being, life-span, or individual (*pudgala*). It is without grasping or relinquishing; it is not seen or heard; it is not perceived or known. This is called receiving and upholding all dharmas."
"Furthermore, noble son!

Moreover, the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī refers to upholding the fact that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty—like what is seen in a dream, like a water bubble, like a mirage, and like space."

Furthermore, one is able to uphold all dharmas as suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and quiescence; their intrinsic nature is unconditioned, being without pleasure and without pain, and without attainment or realization.
Furthermore, the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī is like the great earth, which can support the world—whether large or small—and sustains it all without ever becoming weary.

It is likewise with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who attains the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī: for the sake of sentient beings, they resolve upon bodhicitta, gathering all roots of goodness so that they are not lost or scattered, remaining without even a moment’s slackening or retreat throughout incalculable kalpas.
"Furthermore, just as the great earth can nurture and sustain all things, so too can a Bodhisattva who has attained *dhāraṇī* transform and benefit all sentient beings.

Moreover, just as the great earth can produce grasses and trees to nourish sentient beings, so too can a Bodhisattva who has attained *dhāraṇī* give birth to all wholesome dharmas to benefit sentient beings."
Furthermore, just as the great earth neither increases nor decreases, sustaining all things without being high or low;
so too is the mind of a bodhisattva who has attained dhāraṇī: it neither increases nor decreases, sustaining all sentient beings without the notion of enemy or friend.
Furthermore, just as the great earth never tires of receiving sweet rain,
so too a bodhisattva who has attained dhāraṇī never tires of lovingly delighting in hearing and receiving the teachings of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, just as the great earth can sustain all seeds, causing them to grow according to the seasons without ever ceasing;
so too, the Bodhisattva who has attained *dhāraṇī* can sustain the seeds of all wholesome dharmas, causing them to grow according to the seasons without ever ceasing.
Furthermore, just as a valiant warrior in the world possesses great power and strength and is able to subdue the armies of others,
so too does a Bodhisattva who has attained dhāraṇī possess great diligence, supernatural powers, and majestic virtue, and is able to subdue the armies of Māra.

"Furthermore, son of good family, you should know that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is without forgetting and without anything to be remembered or kept in mind; it is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither suffering nor happiness, neither pure nor impure, neither self nor non-self, neither sentient being nor non-sentient being, neither life-span nor non-life-span, neither person (pudgala) nor non-person, and so forth."
The dharma-gate of dhāraṇī is likewise: there is no recollection, for all dharmas are free from dualistic characteristics and thus there is nothing to forget.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The dharma-gate of dhāraṇī is like space: it sustains the great earth, yet has no notion of that which is sustained;
it upholds all dharmas, yet has no characteristic of that which is upheld.
Furthermore, just as the light of the sun illuminates all forms, so too can dhāraṇī observe and illuminate all dharmas.
Furthermore, just as sentient beings can maintain all seeds of affliction without ever losing them,
so too can the dhāraṇī gateway maintain all dharmas without ever losing them.
Furthermore, just as the mind-reading wheel of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can turn the minds and intentions of all sentient beings, yet lacks any characteristic of "turning";
so too does the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī sustain all phenomena, yet lacks any characteristic of "sustaining."
“O sons of good family!

Just as the various parables previously explained are inexhaustible, so too are all phenomena inexhaustible; this Dharma-door of dhāraṇī is likewise inexhaustible, being immeasurable and boundless like space.”
At that time, while the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was preaching this Dharma, five hundred bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the assembly attained the great dhāraṇīs.
[End of] the third fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-adbhuta-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*.
