under Imperial Edict. At that time, during the middle watch of the night, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again proclaimed the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka for the sake of the various bodhisattvas, addressing them as follows:
“O Great Beings! You must thoroughly understand the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

There is not a single dharma that is not subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; for all dharmas—whether mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, wholesome or unwholesome, with signs or signless, outflowing or without outflows—are all the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.”

“Good son! For example, within this trichiliocosm there are ten billion sets of four great continents, ten billion suns and moons, ten billion Mount Sumerus, and ten billion great oceans; all of these are subsumed within the trichiliocosm and do not exist apart from it.”

The Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is likewise: all dharmas of ordinary beings, dharmas of śrāvakas, dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, and even the dharmas of all Buddhas are not apart from being subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Why is this so? Because the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Buddha vehicle are all one and the same.
It is like a great tree: although its trunk, stalks, branches, and leaves are dense and luxuriant, they all originate from a single root.
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is the foundation from which the teachings of the Three Vehicles arise; it is without distinction or difference, and its magnitude is so vast that it cannot be measured.

"For example, the great ocean is boundlessly expansive; even if the Asura kings, the yakṣas, and even the most powerful mahāsattvas were to attempt to measure it by scooping out its waters, they could never know its limit.
Likewise, all the assemblies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, humans, devas, and others who seek to know the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka can never exhaust it."

Even those who possess wisdom and wish to know the dharmas of a bodhisattva’s ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom cannot know them, for they are known only by those who have entered the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like all sentient beings dwelling within the great ocean who drink only the water of the great ocean and no longer perceive the taste of rivers;
those who cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle know only the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and no longer take pleasure in the paths of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."

“Good son! Within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they are nominally designated as three because of the differences between Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas: those who hear only the principle of the Four Noble Truths and proceed toward the realization of Nirvāṇa are called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
those who delight only in the principle of dependent origination and proceed toward the realization of Nirvāṇa are called the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka.”
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka is so called because it realizes the all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) of a Buddha.

Furthermore, son of good family, you should know that the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka, and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka are equal and without distinction; it is only according to the inclinations and desires of sentient beings' minds that there are trainings in the three vehicles.

Those who study and seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka possess narrow and inferior wisdom and lack the capacity for vast receptivity; fearing the suffering of saṃsāra, they take deep delight in the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and strive to realize nirvāṇa for the sake of seeking peace and security.

Those who delight in seeking the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha have minds that are limited and obstructed; they are unable to act universally for the sake of all sentient beings, and lacking great compassion, they do not practice altruistic deeds, taking the realization of that nirvāṇa as their ultimate goal.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas study the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, its scope is so vast that it cannot be fathomed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; only those Bodhisattvas who cultivate and study these teachings are able to fully comprehend them.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas delight only in their own vehicles; they cultivate various roots of goodness seeking the fruits of the two vehicles, yet they are unable to understand the Dharma of the bodhisattvas."

The bodhisattvas contemplate the teachings of the śrāvakas and are fully able to realize and know the path of the Four Noble Truths; they are well able to discern them, yet they do not proceed to realize their fruits.

They contemplate the teachings of the pratyekabuddhas and are fully able to realize and know the twelve links of dependent origination; they are well able to discern them, yet they do not proceed to realize their fruits.
The Bodhisattvas fulfill all practices and attain complete penetration.
It is like a vessel made of pure lapis lazuli: whatever objects are placed within it all become one color, translucent and without distinction;
likewise, the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, when entering the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, are fundamentally without difference.

Therefore, once the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have entered the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they perceive the equality of all phenomena as being without distinction; there is no characteristic of the Buddha-dharmas, no characteristic of the bodhisattva-dharmas, and no characteristic of the dharma of the Two Vehicles.
Regarding all phenomena, they harbor no thoughts or recollections; they are free from all speech and writing, without expression and without demonstration.
Why is this? Because it is signless, it cannot be observed;
because it is without referent, it cannot be conceptualized.
One who trains in this manner encompasses all-knowledge.
Son of good family!
This is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; one who thus penetrates it attains mastery and is unimpeded.
At that time, during the final watch of the night, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī further proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the irreversible wheel of Dharma of vajra-words.
He addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is skilled in expounding the Dharma, those who hear and understand it—both speaker and listener—all attain the dharma of non-retrogression; they are immovable and cannot be scattered or destroyed."
“Good son! The dharma of non-retrogression—whether it be the vehicle, the sphere of the vehicle, the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha—all are the wheel of non-retrogression.”
Why is this? Because that which is the wheel of non-retrogression is the dharma-realm itself, and it arises from nowhere apart from the dharma-realm.
That wheel has no characteristic of turning; this is called "turning the wheel of the Dharma. It is without distinction and without duality, for it is the very self-nature of the dharma-realm.
"Good son! For this reason, those who practice the path of the bodhisattvas should understand it in this way, whereby they will attain the wheel of non-retrogression that leads to liberation.

Once a bodhisattva mahāsattva has thus understood and attained such liberation, he shall realize the fruit of a Tathāgata and be universally able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings."
Within the gates of liberation, no dualistic phenomena can be apprehended, for the mark of the Tathāgata’s liberation and the mark of the liberation of all phenomena are entirely non-different.
All phenomena lack the mark of liberation and likewise lack the mark of duality.
Why is this? The body is not liberation, and the mind is also not liberation, because the intrinsic nature of these two dharmas is itself the characteristic of liberation;
all dharmas are likewise so.
When Bodhisattvas understand this in such a way, it is the wheel of non-retrogression.
"Good son, you should know:
the wheel of non-retrogression does not turn."
Why is this? Because form and the intrinsic nature of form are fundamentally without any transformation;
likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—the intrinsic nature of consciousness as well—is without any transformation.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is such that nothing therein can be turned back;

this is the wheel of non-retrogression. This wheel is fundamentally indestructible; it is neither with marks nor without marks, neither attainable nor unattainable, neither expressible nor inexpressible, and is without name and without attachment.
"Furthermore, the characteristics of the gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—are dharmas that cannot be differentiated.
From what could they be obtained?
All those characteristics are like space; they have nothing upon which to rely."
The self-nature of all phenomena abides without dependence; this is called the vajra-word, the wheel of non-retrogression. "Good son!
The emptiness of all phenomena is indestructible."
Those vajra-terms are free from all views; one should thus abide in the gate of liberation of emptiness.
Those vajra-terms are free from all conceptual discrimination; one should thus abide in the gate of liberation of signlessness.
Those vajra-terms are free from all doubt and confusion; one should thus abide in the gate of liberation of wishlessness.
That vajra-phrase is free from all attachments and grasping; one should abide in the dharmadhātu in this manner.

As for the vajra-phrase: it is free from manifold phenomena, being without self and without agency, without craving and without attachment; its intrinsic nature abides in the purity of nirvāṇa—this is called the vajra-phrase.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, having expounded various teachings to the bodhisattvas throughout the first, middle, and latter parts of that very night, caused all those bodhisattvas to attain this Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of Radiant Flowers.

Each of those bodhisattvas raised their entire bodies, and from within their pores issued forth hundreds of thousands of rays of light. From each ray of light emerged hundreds of thousands of buddhas, and each of those buddhas extensively performed buddha-deeds for the sake of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
At that time, the King of Magadha, having prepared various kinds of food and drink, came to the place where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was in the early morning and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Now is the very hour; please go and accept my offerings."
The Bodhisattva accepted the invitation, and the king immediately returned to his palace.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having dressed in his robes and taken up his alms bowl at the hour of eating, was about to enter the great city of Rājagṛha with five hundred bhikṣus to beg for food in succession. On the way, a thought arose in his mind:
"I shall not enter this city now; I shall instead go to the place of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī to listen to and receive the True Dharma."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went together with the assembly of bhikṣus to the place where the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was.
Upon arrival, they were filled with joy; they paid their respects, inquired after his well-being, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, saying: "Kāśyapa,
for what reason do you stand here with your alms-bowl at the time of eating?"
Kāśyapa replied, “I intended to enter the great city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms, which is why I have come here first.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
“I shall provide you and the bhikṣus who have come with you with food and drink. Kāśyapa replied, “No.”
“O Bodhisattva!
I have come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma, not to seek food and drink. Mañjuśrī said:
“Venerable sir, you should know that there are two kinds of sustenance for those who seek the Way:
first, food and drink; second, the sublime Dharma.”
Kāśyapa said: "So it is, Great Being!"
“If sentient beings in the world were deprived of edible food, they would not be sustained; unable to nourish their physical bodies, how could they listen to and receive the sublime Dharma?
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī said, “Venerable One, please accept this food and drink; I shall offer it to you.”
Having performed such giving, one neither departs from saṃsāra nor realizes nirvāṇa; one neither leaves behind the dharmas of ordinary beings nor abides in the dharmas of the noble path. Why is this?
The gift given and the giver do not increase or decrease; there is no dharma that can arise and no dharma that can cease; there is no dharma to be learned, nor is there anything to be attained.
"Therefore, I shall give you food and drink.
Kāśyapa addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent! The Bodhisattva is a great donor; such giving as this is true generosity."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī thought to himself:
"I shall now enter the great city of Rājagṛha to perform a great Buddha-work for the sake of the King of Magadha."

Having formed this thought, he immediately entered the samādhi of all supernatural transformations (*sarvābhijñāvikurvaṇa*). Within this samādhi, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the Sahā world-system in its entirety, such that he beheld the trichiliocosm as clearly as looking into the palm of his hand.

All beings in the hells and among the animals who were touched by this light were freed from suffering; not a single sentient being gave rise to the three poisons, nor did they harbor thoughts of hatred, jealousy, or resentment, but instead regarded one another with mutual affection as a child regards its mother.
The entire trichiliocosm shook in six ways.

At that time, the devaputras of the desire and form realms all came to make offerings to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva; they played hundreds of thousands of kinds of music and rained down exquisite celestial flowers, scattering them upon the road as an adornment.

The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, by means of his supernormal powers, caused the road to become entirely level like the palm of a hand and adorned it with countless precious jewels; he scattered various exquisite flowers as large as chariot wheels—namely, utpala, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers.
Furthermore, he covered the area above with jeweled nets and canopies, and spread various banners, streamers, and parasols until they filled the void of space.

He further manifested terraces made of the seven treasures and various jewel trees; upon these jewel trees were flowers and fruits made of vaidūrya, interlaced with cords of various jewels. From each individual jewel tree issued a subtle and wondrous fragrance that pervaded an entire yojana.

Between those trees there are further jewel ponds with sands of gold spread across their bottoms, filled with water possessing the eight virtues. From them emerge various exquisite flowers—namely, the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka—and there also dwell and sport pairs of mandarin ducks, ruddy sheldrakes, wild ducks, and geese.
All the jewel trees and jewel terraces were filled with exquisite fragrances, which brought joy to all who smelled them.
Beneath each tree stood twenty-five great goddesses, who made offerings by holding *candana* sandalwood incense.
After the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had manifested such extraordinary wonders within that samādhi, he emerged from the meditative absorption and addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"I shall now go with you to the royal palace of the King of Magadha in the great city of Rājagṛha to receive the offering of a meal."
"The senior of great virtue should lead the way; I shall surely follow behind. Kāśyapa replied, "No."
Bodhisattva!

Great Being, you are endowed with great wisdom, immeasurable supernatural powers, extensive learning, and eloquence; you skillfully expound all dharmas and are constantly praised by our Buddha, the World-Honored One. When sentient beings see you, they give rise to the bodhicitta and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.
"Although I am called an elder among the assembly of śrāvakas, I possess no such capability; how would I dare to walk before you?
I wish to follow behind the Bodhisattva."

Why is this? Because when all sentient beings first resolve their minds toward Bodhi, they already surpass all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; how much more so those who have long practiced the Bodhisattva path?
For example, a lion cub possesses great strength from the moment of birth; it is courageous, agile, and fearless.
When the fragrance of its body is carried by the wind, all the various beasts who smell it are struck with terror.
Even the great elephant, though possessing great power that none in the world can subdue, is likewise filled with fear upon smelling the scent of the newborn lion.

If sentient beings give rise to the bodhicitta with such courage and firmness that all Māras and sentient beings conceive thoughts of fear toward them, they cannot be surpassed by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
When the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear the Buddha preach the Mahāyāna Dharma, their minds remain unmoved; they give rise to great joy and are able to let out the lion’s roar, subduing all beings.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!
Within the true Dharma there are no three vehicles; rather, the bodhicitta alone is the sovereign, for all wholesome dharmas arise from the bodhicitta.
"Now, as the Bodhisattva proceeds before us, it is as if the Bodhicitta gives rise to immeasurable wholesome dharmas.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī walked at the head, surrounded on all sides by the great Bodhisattvas, while the assembly of Śrāvakas followed behind him; they departed from their original dwelling place and entered the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, various flowers rained down from the heavens, and hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments played in the void. A great radiance was emitted, illuminating the entire assembly, and within that light, various lotus flowers fell like rain.
When all the people in the city of Rājagṛha saw the Bodhisattva, they were filled with joy and offered worship by bringing various fragrant flowers.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha heard that the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, together with a multitude of eighty thousand great Bodhisattvas and five hundred śrāvakas, had come to attend the assembly. He then thought to himself:
"I have prepared five hundred portions of food and drink; now this assembly of Bodhisattvas and others is many times greater in number. How will these few provisions suffice?"
"Furthermore, where might he be accommodated so that he may sit?

While he was thinking this, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī immediately commanded the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa and the Great Yakṣa Lord Cūḍapanthaka to manifest in the form of a youth within a single kṣaṇa and go before the king, saying to him: "Great King!"
Do not give rise to anxiety.

The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī possesses great skillful means; his merit and wisdom are inconceivable. He is able to universally provide a single meal for all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm so that they are all fully satisfied, yet the food remains inexhaustible.
Now, these eighty thousand bodhisattvas and five hundred śrāvakas are not many in number; what need is there for concern?
Why is this? Because the merit and wisdom of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī are fundamentally inexhaustible, his food is likewise inexhaustible.

At that time, having heard these words, the King of Magadha was filled with great joy, delight, and happiness. He immediately conceived a sense of reverence, respect, and wonder toward the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and together with his court and retinue, he took fragrant flowers, powdered incense, and unguents, and accompanied by various musical performances, went out to welcome the Bodhisattva.
Having seen him, they prostrated, knelt, and inquired after his well-being; scattering fragrant flowers, they escorted the Bodhisattva into the royal palace.
At that time, once the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had arrived at the royal palace, he addressed the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha, saying:
"O Son of Good Family!
"You should adorn the site of enlightenment; now is precisely the right time.

Having received this command, the Bodhisattva Universal Radiance, by means of his supernormal powers, caused the king’s palace to suddenly become vast, expansive, and pure. Adorned with various ornaments without any obstruction, with flower canopies, banners, and necklaces suspended from it, it was made the supreme site of enlightenment, most exquisitely decorated.
He further addressed the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, saying: "Good son!
You should prepare a most excellent seat for me and provide seating for the great assembly."

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata made the gesture of snapping his fingers to summon them; in an instant, eighty-three thousand exquisite seats appeared within the site of enlightenment, adorned with various kinds of precious jewels, and though these seats filled the entire site, there was no crowding.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī took his seat and commanded the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas to each take their respective seats.
Then, the King of Magadha approached the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and said:
"I pray that the Bodhisattva and the great assembly will show me compassion by waiting a short while; food and drink are about to arrive."

At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues, came to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to pay homage, show reverence, and make offerings to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and the great assembly.

Furthermore, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with his retinue and the retinues of the asuras, each brought sandalwood and powdered incense to the site of enlightenment to make offerings to the great assembly.

Furthermore, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world-system, manifested the form of a youth and, together with his retinue of Brahma-devas and attendants, each holding a precious whisk, came to the site of enlightenment; having paid homage to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, he stood by his side.
The various Brahmā assemblies who had come also held precious whisks and stood to the right of the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

Furthermore, the Dragon King Anavatapta came to the site of enlightenment and remained in mid-air without manifesting his body; he suspended various necklaces from which flowed water of eight virtues, which the entire great assembly used without it ever being exhausted.
At that time, King Magadha thought to himself:
"These bodhisattvas all lack alms bowls; with what shall they eat?
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, knowing the king's thoughts, addressed him, saying:
"Do not think that these bodhisattvas do not carry alms bowls.
When they require a bowl, whatever vessel is appropriate for their buddha-field will arrive spontaneously."
The King was greatly delighted and immediately addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"In which Buddha-fields do these bodhisattvas dwell?
From where have they come?"
"I wish to hear the names of the lands from which these bodhisattvas have come,
as well as the names of their Buddhas. Mañjuśrī replied,
"Great King, you should know this:"
To the east there is a land named Constant Sound; there the Buddha known as Auspicious Sound Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, currently dwells and teaches the Dharma.
"These bodhisattvas have come from that world to receive the King’s offerings, and they shall also cause the Great King to behold a rare marvel.

At that moment, eighty-three thousand precious bowls were sent from the world of Constant Sound; through the majestic spiritual power of that Buddha and the power of the vows and practices of those bodhisattvas, those bowls came through the air to this Sahā world and arrived at Lake Anavatapta.
Immediately, eighty-three thousand dragon maidens purified their bowls with water possessing the eight virtues and each brought them before the bodhisattvas.
At that time, King Magadha, having witnessed this event, marveled at its inconceivability and unprecedented nature, and his heart was filled with great joy.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the king, saying:
"The vessels for the bodhisattvas have now arrived; Your Majesty should distribute food and drink to provide for the entire assembly."
Then the king immediately presented the various foods and drinks he had prepared to the Bodhisattva and the great assembly.

At that time, the entire multitude at the site of enlightenment was fully satisfied; not a single person lacked anything, yet when they looked at the food and drink, it still appeared not to have been exhausted.
The King addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"How marvelous, Great Being!
Although I offered my meager food to the entire assembly, it is still not exhausted."
The Bodhisattva replied: "Great King!
The true Dharma is inexhaustible, and that from which food arises is likewise inexhaustible."
At that time, when the great assembly of bodhisattvas had finished their meal, they cast their alms bowls toward the sky, where they remained suspended without moving.
The king addressed the Bodhisattva,
saying, "In what do these bowls rest?"
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Great King, does the true Dharma have any abiding place?
The King replied:
“The true Dharma should have no place of abiding.
The Bodhisattva said:
“Great King, you should know this:”
The true Dharma has no abiding place, and this bowl likewise has no abiding place.
If the bowl has no abiding place, all phenomena are also thus.
Great King, you should know this:
"Because the nature of phenomena is empty, one should abide in this manner.

At that time, King Magadha, having made offerings to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and the great assembly, stood before the Bodhisattva with a heart of yearning and a desire to hear his Dharma. He then addressed Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:
"O Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, could you please explain to me the rare and marvelous Dharma?"
The Bodhisattva replied: "Great King!

As for this rare Dharma, even if Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to speak of it for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they could never exhaust it."
Upon hearing this, the king was seized with alarm and dread; he became bewildered and unhappy.
Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the king: "Do not say:
"Could even Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges not proclaim such a rare and marvelous Dharma, and could the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī likewise not speak it?
It is simply that the Dharma of all Buddhas is inexhaustible and beyond the reach of verbal expression."

"You should simply ask Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva whatever you desire; for this Great Being, through the power of his immeasurable skillful means, will surely be able to explain rare and wondrous teachings to the King."
Having heard these words, his mind was suddenly awakened, and he addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"Just now, upon hearing what the Bodhisattva said, doubt arose in my heart; by receiving your words, I have become slightly awakened."
He then stepped forward and addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "Bodhisattva!
Why is it that even Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cannot proclaim such a rare and marvelous Dharma?"
Upon hearing these words, my mind was at a loss for what to do; I only pray that the Bodhisattva will resolve my doubts.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied: “Great King!
The Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are not unable to speak of rare and marvelous dharmas; yet that no dharma is spoken is itself the rare and marvelous dharma.
Great King, regarding all dharmas, one should simply have a mind that dwells nowhere; for those dharmas cannot be spoken of, nor can the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, be spoken of.
"Great King!
Do you perceive any signs in the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones?
The King replied:
"No. He asked again: "Can the arising of the mind be seen?"
"Can the cessation of the mind be seen? He replied, "No."
He asked again:
"Can conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena, true phenomena and false phenomena, all be seen?
The King replied:
"All are unobservable.
The Bodhisattva asked:
"Regarding all dharmas, is there any characteristic to be observed, or is there anything to be spoken of?"
The King said, "No. Mañjuśrī said:
"Great King! For this reason, I have said:
'This is a rare dharma that Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cannot fully proclaim.'"
"Furthermore, Great King!
Space is without characteristics and is also without movement or change; it cannot be defiled by smoke, clouds, dust, or mist."
The intrinsic nature of space is pure; no phenomenon can defile it, nor can any phenomenon purify it. All Buddhas and Tathāgatas realize that all phenomena are equal to space.
For this reason, even the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, could not exhaustively describe it.
"Furthermore, Great King, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, remain immovable within the state of non-abiding; they act while remaining eternally quiescent."
Why is this? Because phenomena cannot be transmigrated, as they are free from the distinction between proper and improper locations;
because phenomena cannot be apprehended, as they are free from all grasping at signs.

Great King, you should know that all phenomena are neither born nor unborn; they are neither great nor small; they are neither real nor unreal; they are neither with perception nor without perception; they are neither active nor inactive; they are neither wise nor foolish; they are neither grasping at signs nor not grasping at signs; they are neither accumulated nor dispersed; they are without coming or going; they are neither inverted nor free from inversion; they are neither identical to afflictions nor separate from afflictions; and they are neither self-arisen nor produced by another.
“Great King! All phenomena are like space, because they are without movement or change;
all phenomena are peerless, because they are free from companions.”
All dharmas lack dual characteristics because they are without differentiation;
all dharmas have no boundaries because they cannot be seen;
all dharmas have no measure because they are neither large nor small.
All phenomena are inexhaustible, for they are constantly in motion;
all phenomena are vast, for they pervade the dharma-realm;
all phenomena have no place of abiding, for they exist neither internally, nor externally, nor in between.
All phenomena are without discrimination, for they are free from conceptual construction;
all phenomena are eternal, for they are subject to no change or transformation;
all phenomena are blissful, for they are devoid of suffering and affliction.
All phenomena possess a sovereign, for they are free from deluded attachment;
all phenomena are pure, for they are not defiled;
all phenomena are quiescent, for they are eternally serene.
All phenomena are unattainable because they are free from the mark of self;
all phenomena are not objects of delight because they have the mark of liberation;
all phenomena are neither "this" nor "that" because they are free from the grasping of a self.
All phenomena are indestructible, for they are free from manifold characteristics;
all phenomena are of a single flavor, for they share the nature of liberation;
all phenomena have a single characteristic, for they are free from all notions of difference.
All phenomena are empty, because they are free from all views;
all phenomena are signless, because their signs are pure;
all phenomena are wishless, because they are free from the three periods of time.
All phenomena are not encompassed by the three periods of time, for the past, present, and future cannot be apprehended.
Birth and death and nirvana are fundamentally equal; all phenomena are equal.
"Great King!
Since all phenomena are thus, can afflictions and doubts arise?
The King said:
"No. Since all phenomena are empty, how could there be afflictions or doubts?
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.

“Afflictions are non-arising and dharmas are likewise unspeakable; the nature of afflictions is empty, and all dharmas are equal. Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are fundamentally equal, and afflictions and bodhi are also equal.”
The Sūtra on the Unprecedented True Dharma Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
The Sūtra on the Unprecedented True Dharma Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
The Great Master Dengyō, the Subject Hōten, translated by Imperial Decree:
“Furthermore, Great King!

There is a rare dharma, profound and difficult to understand, namely the mark of the quiescence of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śānta-lakṣaṇa*). It is neither grasped nor abandoned; it is neither accumulated nor dispersed. Arising from causes and conditions, it possesses no sovereign master.”
Because they arise dependently, phenomena are neither self-produced nor produced by another.
All phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because their intrinsic nature is empty, they are non-apprehensible.
Due to this non-apprehensibility, all phenomena are quiescent.
"O Great King! The characteristic of tranquility is the characteristic of reality.
You should give rise to right faith and train yourself thus, and observe thus."
One who trains in this manner is free from all marks; there is neither that which is learned nor that which is not learned, and there is neither gain nor loss.
To understand things in this way is right liberation; the characteristic of liberation is precisely all dharmas.
The emptiness of the nature of all phenomena is the true meaning; it is without attachment and without limitation or obstruction, and is thus called the most supreme and rare dharma.
"Furthermore, Great King, you should know:
the faculty of the eye is neither defiled nor pure."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the eye-faculty is fundamentally real;
likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties are neither defiled nor pure, for their intrinsic natures are fundamentally real.
"Great King!
Form is neither defiled nor pure;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither defiled nor pure."
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the aggregates (*skandha*) is fundamentally real.
This applies even to all phenomena (*dharma*): they are neither defiled nor pure, for their intrinsic nature is real.
“Great King, you should know this:
the mind has no form or appearance; it is not something that can be observed by the eye.
The mind has no place of abiding; it cannot be found within, without, or in between.”
Why is this? The intrinsic nature of the mind is neither defiled nor pure; it neither increases nor decreases, and it is without movement or change.
Therefore, Great King!
"You should contemplate this as it truly is; do not give rise to doubt, but abide in the true Dharma.
Because this mind is real, all phenomena are likewise so. Great King!"
For example, space is free from all forms and characteristics, and it is devoid of movement or change.
If someone were to say:
"I am able to stain this space with smoke, clouds, dust, or mist," [it would be impossible].
"Would this be considered credible? The king replied, "No."
"Space has no marks because it cannot be defiled.
The Bodhisattva said, "The mind is also like this: it is pure from the beginning and does not receive any defilements."
Even so, the self-nature of all phenomena is likewise unstained.
"Furthermore, Great King, all phenomena and the Dharma-realm are neither identical nor separate; their fundamental nature is equal and without distinction."
"If one understands this, then regarding all phenomena there will be no obstruction, nor any increase or decrease.

When the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī spoke these teachings, King Magadha realized the emptiness of the nature of phenomena and was filled with great joy. He immediately attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and, giving rise to a sense of rare wonder, joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"The great compassion and skillful means of the Bodhisattvas are such that the Dharma you have taught is truly rare, subtle, profound, and far-reaching—something never heard before."
"Today I have severed all doubts and my mind has attained clarity.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said, "Great King!"
Do not say, "Doubt has been eliminated.
One who speaks thus has not severed all marks; for there to be marks within the mind is itself a great doubt.

"Great King, you should know that all phenomena are quiescent: they are without speech and without demonstration, without hearing and without attainment; how could there be any doubt to be eliminated?"
The King said: “Bodhisattva!
If this is so, then should all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion not obstruct the mind?”
The Bodhisattva said: "Great King!
That which I previously stated:"
"Space is fundamentally pure, for it cannot be defiled.
Such is its meaning, Great King!
The mind is fundamentally pure, and the nature of afflictions is empty; since neither can be apprehended, what could possibly obstruct it?
Therefore, one should not give rise to thoughts of sinful defilements within the mind.
Great King, you should know:
the past mind is unattainable, the future mind is unattainable, and the present mind is unattainable;

even so it is with all phenomena. Within the three periods of time, they neither come nor go, neither abide nor cling; they have no point of entry and no place of return, being free from all false conceptualizations and beyond the reach of knowledge and vision.
"That which is free from the dharma of knowing and seeing is what the Buddha has taught.
Therefore, the wise should contemplate in this way and understand it thus.
At that time, the Great King addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

“As the Bodhisattva has explained, I now understand that the intrinsic nature of the mind and the intrinsic nature of all phenomena are fundamentally pure; they are not defiled by obscurations, nor is there any characteristic to be apprehended.”
"Therefore, I have now attained indestructible faith before this Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva said, "Great King!"
"If it is thus, this is itself liberation, free from all faults.

At that time, King Magadha, having heard the sublime Dharma proclaimed by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, was filled with great joy. He rose from his seat, took a superior, fine cotton cloth worth hundreds of thousands, and went before the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī to present it to him, wishing to clothe the Bodhisattva’s body with that cloth.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva vanished from sight in an instant; however, a voice was heard from the air, saying:
"Great King! The signs you have perceived are not what I have received."
As for my receiving, I do not perceive my own body nor the bodies of others; there is no giver and no gift.
Even so it is with all phenomena: they are devoid of perceptible characteristics and free from the mind of grasping and attachment.
"Great King!
If there is anyone who can see their own body, you should give this cotton cloth to them.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Jñānaketu; the king immediately took the cloth and offered it to him as a gift.
That bodhisattva said: "Great King!
Any perceived signs are not what I accept."

As I am a recipient, I do not cling to ordinary beings or the dharmas of ordinary beings; I do not abide in those in training or the dharmas of those in training; I do not realize the state of those beyond training or the dharmas of those beyond training; I do not proceed toward pratyekabuddhas or the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas; nor do I seek the liberation and nirvana of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas as a fruit to be realized.
Thus, regarding all phenomena, one is without signs of attachment; both the giver and the recipient are pure, such that there is neither profit nor gain.
It is only when one gives in this manner that they may receive.
At that time, the Great King wished to clothe the Bodhisattva’s body with the cotton cloth, but the Bodhisattva immediately made his body invisible. Only the voice from the air was heard, saying:
"If there is anyone who can see my body, then you may give it to them."
At that time, there was another bodhisattva named Śāntavimokṣa; the king immediately took a piece of fine cotton cloth and offered it to him.
That bodhisattva said, “Great King!...”
Any perceived characteristics are not what I accept.

As I accept them, neither the view of self nor the view of "mine" arises; they are neither afflictions nor free from afflictions, neither abiding in a concentrated mind nor giving rise to distraction, neither wisdom nor folly, being free from all grasping and rejecting.
"One who gives in such a manner may accept it.
At that time, the Great King wished to drape the cotton cloth over the Bodhisattva’s body, but the Bodhisattva immediately made his body invisible. Only a voice was heard from the air, saying:
"If there is one who can see my body, then you may give it to them."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Paramamanasikāra; the king immediately took a piece of fine cotton cloth and offered it to him.
That bodhisattva said:
"Great King!..."
Any perceived signs are not what I accept. As for how I accept them:
no signs arise; one does not engage in bodily action, does not initiate vocal action, does not give rise to mental action, and does not cling to the phenomena of the aggregates, bases, or elements.
One realizes that all phenomena are unattainable; they are not known by wisdom, nor can they be reached by words. They have no basis of reliance and are as serene as empty space.
A donor who acts in this manner is one from whom [the recipient] may accept.

At that time, the great king wished to clothe the Bodhisattva’s body with the cotton cloth, but the Bodhisattva immediately made his body invisible so that it could not be seen; only a voice was heard saying:
"If there is anyone who can see my body, then you may give it to them."
There was another bodhisattva named Uttaramati; the king immediately took a piece of fine cotton cloth and offered it to him.
That bodhisattva said, "Great King!..."
Any perceived marks are not what I accept.
If I were to accept them as I do now, I would not give rise to a mind that grasps at marks or harbors longing.
If one says they have resolved their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this constitutes grasping at marks and having something to long for.
Why is this? Because the mind that is free from signs is the very mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; since this mind is equal, the bodhicitta is also equal.
This bodhicitta is the mind of all Tathāgatas. By virtue of this equality, all dharmas are equal—non-dual, without distinction, without grasping, and without abandoning.
Because of being free from grasping and abandoning, the notion of a self does not arise;
once the notion of a self has ceased, there is nothing to be sought.
A gift given in such a manner may be accepted.

At that time, the Great King wished to clothe the Bodhisattva’s body with the cotton cloth; however, the Bodhisattva immediately made his body invisible and did not appear, but a voice was heard saying:
"If there is anyone who can see my body, then you may give it to them."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Samādhyunmīlitapuṣpa; the king immediately took a piece of fine cotton cloth and offered it to him.
That bodhisattva said, "Great King!..."
Any perceived signs are not what I accept.
As for how I accept them: having realized all gateways of samādhi as signless and non-conceptual, one understands that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is immovable—this is samādhi.
"One who gives in such a manner may accept it.
At that time, the Great King wished to drape the cotton cloth over the Bodhisattva’s body, but the Bodhisattva immediately made his body invisible and did not appear.
He only heard a voice say:
"If there is anyone who can see my body, they may receive this gift.
There was another bodhisattva named Siddhārtha; the king immediately took the cotton cloth and offered it to him.
The Bodhisattva said: "Great King!
Any perceived signs are not what I accept."
As I receive it, one understands that the intrinsic nature of all language and written characters is fundamentally empty, devoid of any characteristics of attachment.
Indeed, those who wish to give rise to the mind to seek after dharmas fall into the midst of signs of existence and cannot be said to achieve accomplishment.
If one realizes that all phenomena are unattainable, then all purposes are accomplished and everything is as desired.
Such a donor may accept [the gift].
At that time, the Great King wished to clothe the Bodhisattva’s body with the cotton cloth, but the Bodhisattva immediately made his body invisible. Only a voice was heard, saying:
"If there is anyone who can see my body, then you may give it to them."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Trimaṇḍalapariśuddha; the king immediately took a piece of fine cotton cloth and offered it to him.
That bodhisattva said, "Great King!..."
Any perceived characteristic is not what I accept as mine.

If it were as I accept it, there would be no one capable of giving and no one capable of receiving; the receiver would have nothing obtained and the giver would have no karmic fruit. I myself would not exist, and that which belongs to me (*mama*) would likewise be empty.
"One who gives in such a manner may accept it.
The king then took the cotton cloth and wished to clothe his body, but at that moment the Bodhisattva made himself invisible; he heard only a voice say:
"If there were anyone able to see my body, then you might give it to them."
Furthermore, there was a bodhisattva named Dharmavikurvaṇa; the king immediately took a piece of fine cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) and offered it to him.
That bodhisattva said, "Great King!..."
Whatever marks are perceived are not what I accept.

As for what I accept, one does not take the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas as the fruit of realization, nor does one take the great parinirvāṇa as the fruit of realization; one neither departs from the dharmas of saṃsāra nor seeks the dharmas of nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equal.
One who gives in such a manner may accept [the gift].
The king then took the cotton cloth, intending to clothe his body; at that moment, the Bodhisattva made himself invisible, and only a voice was heard saying:
"If there is anyone who can see my body, then you may give it to them."
At that time, the Great King offered the cotton cloth he had intended for donation to these various great bodhisattvas; however, they each made their bodies invisible and none accepted it.
Thereupon, the Great King took the cloth and went to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, saying:

"Venerable Kāśyapa, among the śrāvakas you are of advanced age and great virtue, praised by the Buddha as foremost in the dhūta practices. I pray that you will accept this exquisite, fine cotton cloth and fulfill my heart’s intent in giving."
Kāśyapa replied: “Great King!
Any perceived characteristics are not what I accept.”
As I am a recipient, I do not sever greed, hatred, and delusion, yet I am without any defiled attachment;
even up to ignorance and the craving for existence, I do not sever them at all, nor do I associate with them.

There is no seeing of suffering, no abandoning of the origin, no realizing of cessation, and no cultivating of the path; there is no seeing of the Buddha, no hearing of the Dharma, and no entering into the ranks of the assembly; there is no attainment or realization of the knowledge of exhaustion or the knowledge of non-arising; there is no giver, no receiver, no great fruit, and no small fruit; there is no saṃsāra to be weary of, and no nirvāṇa to be realized.
"All dharmas are pure and free from all marks.
A donor such as this may accept [this gift].
The king then took the cotton cloth and wished to clothe his body, but Kāśyapa likewise made himself invisible and did not appear; he was heard only to say:
"If there is anyone who can see my body, I shall give it to them.
Thus, Great King, he offered the cotton cloth to the five hundred great śrāvakas, but they each refused to accept it, concealing their bodies and remaining invisible.
At that time, the Great King had this thought:
"Now these bodhisattvas and śrāvakas all refuse the cotton cloth I have offered; I shall now take it to the inner palace and offer it to my queen and her attendants, for they will surely accept it."
Having formed this thought, he took a piece of fine cotton cloth and entered the palace intending to give it as a gift.
At that time, the Great King did not see his consort; he then thought of giving it to the palace ladies and his kinsmen, but he did not see them either.
In this way, as he gradually observed them, all the palaces and cities, as well as the halls and buildings, ceased to appear entirely, becoming identical to empty space.
At that time, the Great King again thought to himself:
"Now these exquisite and fine cotton cloths no longer have anything upon which to be spread."
Having formed this thought, he wished to take the cotton cloth and clothe his own body with it.
At that moment, the king likewise could not see his own body; he heard only a voice from the air saying:
"If there is anyone who can see their own body, then you may bestow it upon them."
"Great King!
You should observe for yourself where the physical marks and form of your own body now reside.
Just as you observe your own body and do not perceive its marks, so it is with others; the marks of both self and other are entirely unobtainable."
If one views it in this way, one sees the true Dharma; the true Dharma is free from all views, and because it is free from all views, one abides in the Dharma of equality.
At that time, having heard the voice from the sky, the Great King abandoned the mind of perceived characteristics and severed all thoughts of doubt, awakening as if rising from sleep.

Immediately, the palace city, the halls and buildings, the queen, and the retinue saw that his physical appearance had returned to its former state; they then proceeded to where the Bodhisattva and the great assembly were, and all beheld the Bodhisattva’s features exactly as they were before, without any difference.
At that time, the Great King came forward and addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Where is the great assembly of bodhisattvas going, that I do not see them? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Great King! Do not give rise to doubt. This great assembly was originally without coming; where could it possibly go?
Great King!”
"Do you see this assembly now?
The King replied,
"Indeed, I have already seen it."
The Bodhisattva asked, "What did you see? He replied:
"Just as one sees the true Dharma, so too should one contemplate this assembly.
He asked again: "How, then, is this very reality to be seen?"

He replied: "The true Dharma is free from all marks; it is not what is observed by the eye, nor does it exist internally, externally, or in between, for the two dharmas of name and mark cannot be apprehended."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, you should know this:
You previously committed evil deeds, and I have heard the Buddha’s prophecy that in a future age you shall fall into the evil realms."
The king said to the Bodhisattva, “No, Great Being!”
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has never said that there are those who fall into evil destinies or those who realize nirvana.
Why is this? Because within the true Dharma, there is no duality or distinction.
The Bodhisattva spoke again: "No, Great King!"
As the Buddha has taught:
"The retribution for good and evil causes and effects is manifest. What is the meaning of this statement?
The Great King replied:
"O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!

In my view, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, employ skillful means in accordance with circumstances to skillfully teach on saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, causing all sentient beings to weary of the suffering of saṃsāra and incline toward the bliss of nirvāṇa."
To speak according to reality, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are equal. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are empty and lack intrinsic nature.
The nature of those phenomena is the very nature of the Dharma-realm; within the nature of the Dharma-realm, there is no duality or distinction.
For this reason, all phenomena are neither produced nor do they pass away; they are without desire and without aversion or relinquishment.
"I have now given rise to right faith and feel no fear.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said, "Excellent, Great King!"
"You have spoken these words well, being free from all marks of existence.
The King said, "O Bodhisattva!"
The nature of the self is inherently empty; who is there to preach it?
All phenomena are fundamentally without marks; what, then, is there to be relinquished?
As the Buddha has said:

"In the true Dharma, the mark of a self is fundamentally non-existent; it is free from both the sentient and the insentient, and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are without action and without a recipient.
The Bodhisattva said: "Great King!"
"Although you have understood the true Dharma, you still give rise to attachment.
The King spoke again, saying:
"How does one become free from attachment?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"Not destroying the characteristics of the evil realms—this is what is meant by 'non-attachment'.
The King said:
“Bodhisattva! It is so, it is so.
According to my understanding, the characteristics of the evil realms are unshakable; they are neither destroyed nor clung to, and there is nothing to fear.”

I have now attained liberation from all attachments and shall never again give rise to views characterized by signs, just as a Bodhisattva who has attained patience no longer gives rise to thoughts of the three poisons.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu said to the king: "Great King!
You have already attained purity in the path of wisdom, are free from all defilements and stains, and are fully endowed with patience."
The king addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:

"All dharmas are exceedingly pure, vast, and immeasurable; they cannot be defiled by afflictions, and nirvana is unattainable. Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has personally realized and known this."

At that time, while the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and the great beings were preaching the True Dharma within the royal palace, the King of Magadha attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Within that royal palace, there were thirty-two women who, having witnessed the miraculous transformations and supernatural powers of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Within the assembly, there were another five hundred people who attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

All the inhabitants of Rājagṛha city took various famous flowers and exquisite incenses and gathered at the gate of the royal palace, offering worship from afar to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and the great multitude.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, out of compassion for all the people within the city and for their benefit and happiness, pressed the earth with his toe. Immediately, the great earth turned the color of vaidūrya, pure and lustrous, transparent throughout both inside and out.

At that time, all the people within the city, whether men or women, were able to see the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and the great assembly without any obstruction; just as a pure, round mirror reflects one's facial features, so too did all the people behold the countenance of the Bodhisattva.

At that time, when the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had preached the Dharma to each of them according to their needs, eighty-four thousand people within the city attained the pure Dharma-eye, and five hundred people resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī had accepted the meal offering of King Magadha and preached the Dharma extensively for him, all those in the king's retinue as well as all the people attained benefit and happiness; they conceived a sense of rare wonder and gave rise to great joy.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat and, surrounded by the great assembly of bodhisattvas, departed from the royal palace.

At that time, the King of Magadha, together with his ministers, attendants, and retinue, paid their respects and offered words of thanks, following the Bodhisattva to the assembly at the Buddha’s dwelling.
At that time, having departed from the royal palace, the Bodhisattva proceeded by stages; along the way, he saw a man beneath a tree weeping and wailing, uttering these words:
"I have committed the karma of killing, which is most terrifying; in the future, I will certainly fall into hell."
"How may I now obtain deliverance?
At that time, the Bodhisattva, having seen this person, observed that their faculties and conditions were already matured and they were capable of receiving transformation and deliverance.
The Bodhisattva then transformed himself into a person who was indistinguishable from the others; having approached that individual, he also began to weep and said to him:
"I have committed the karma of killing, which is truly terrifying; in the future, I shall certainly fall into hell."
Having heard this, the person immediately said:
"I too have committed the karma of killing; now that we have encountered this moment, who could devise a skillful means to deliver us?"
At that time, the transformed person immediately said to him:
"Now we have committed extremely grave offenses; though we are filled with great terror, there is no one who can save us."
"Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses great skillful means and is able to deliver us; we should now go together to where the Buddha is.
Having spoken thus, the transformed person immediately went forward.
Having seen this, that person also followed him to where the Buddha was.
When the manifested being had reached the assembly of the Buddha, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I have committed the karma of killing and am terrified of falling into hell.
I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will deliver me.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately praised him with these words:
“Excellent, excellent! Son of good family,
you have now uttered words of truth before the Buddha, speaking in accordance with reality regarding what you have done.”
Regarding what you have said about one who commits the act of killing: from what state of mind does the characteristic of the offense arise?
Is it from the past, or is it from the future?
Is it in the present?
If one gives rise to a past mind, the past has already ceased and the mind cannot be apprehended;
if one gives rise to a future mind, the future has not yet arrived and the mind cannot be apprehended.
If one gives rise to a present mind, the present does not abide, and the mind is likewise unattainable.
Since all three periods of time are unattainable, there is neither arising nor activity.
Because there is neither arising nor activity, what characteristic of transgression could possibly be perceived?
“Good son! The mind has no place of abiding; it is not within, without, or in between.
The mind has no form or appearance; it is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white.”
The mind is without contrivance, for there is no agent;
the mind is not an illusion, for it is fundamentally real;
the mind has no boundaries, for it is not limited.
The mind is without grasping or rejecting, for it is neither good nor evil;
the mind is without movement or fluctuation, for it is neither arising nor ceasing;
the mind is equal to empty space, for it is without obstruction.
The mind is neither defiled nor pure, for it is free from all numerical categories. "Good son!
All those who possess wisdom should contemplate in this way; for one who contemplates thus, the mind cannot be found when sought within all phenomena."
Why is this? The intrinsic nature of the mind is the nature of all phenomena; the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena is the true nature.
For this reason, you should not now give rise to groundless fear.
At that time, having heard the Buddha proclaim the Dharma of ultimate truth, the emanated person was filled with great joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
You have skillfully expounded that the intrinsic nature of the dharma-realm is pure; having now realized that the nature of my sinful karma is empty, I feel no fear.
I now desire to leave the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma and maintain the holy life (brahmacarya); I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me his acceptance.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!"
"Now is precisely the right time; I shall accept you.

At that moment, in an instant, the transformed person's hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and with the saṃghāṭī robe covering his body, he took on the appearance of a bhikṣu. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I now wish to enter parinirvāṇa; I pray that the Buddha will grant me his permission.
The Buddha said, "As you wish."

Then, by the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, the emanated bhikṣu leaped into the air to the height of a tala tree; he manifested fire to consume himself, until he was completely extinguished without remainder, becoming one with empty space.
At that time, those who had actually committed the karmic deeds, having seen this manifested person leave the household life and having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, conceived this thought:
"This person committed the same sinful karma as I; since he has already attained liberation, I too should now seek the Buddha’s transformation and deliverance."
Having formed this thought, he immediately prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have committed the karma of killing and am terrified that I shall fall into the great hells in the future; I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will grant me deliverance."
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!”
Now, before the Buddha, I utter these words of truth:
regarding the karma you have created, from what state of mind did it arise?
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of this sinful karma?
At that time, because his roots of goodness had matured, upon hearing the Buddha’s words, great flames issued from all the pores of his body and circled around him. He then spoke these words:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha; I pray that you will grant me deliverance."
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden right hand over the man’s head.

Immediately, the fire on the man’s body was extinguished; he was freed from his suffering and affliction, attained great joy, and, having conceived pure faith, joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“How rare, World-Honored One!”

Previously, I heard the Buddha extensively explain the dharma of the pure dharmadhātu that is free from all characteristics; having now realized that the nature of karmic offenses is empty, I no longer give rise to thoughts of fear.
"I too now wish to leave the household life within the Buddha’s Dharma to practice the holy life; I pray that the Buddha will accept me.
The Buddha said, "Excellent."
"Now is precisely the right time; I shall accept you.

Immediately, this person's hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and a kāṣāya robe was draped over his body, so that he took on the appearance of a bhikṣu—like one of a hundred years' seniority, with his faculties perfectly disciplined, his deportment composed and orderly, and all his aspirations fulfilled.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him.

Having heard the Dharma, he immediately became free from dust and defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye. Furthermore, as he carefully contemplated the principles of the truths, he realized the fruit of Arhatship within the assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I now wish to enter nirvana; I pray that the Buddha will grant me his permission.
The Buddha said, "As you wish."
At that time, the bhikṣu leaped into the air to a height of seven tala trees, transformed his body into fire, and consumed it until nothing remained.
Immediately, hundreds of thousands of devas and humans within the assembly gave rise to a sense of rare wonder and each prostrated themselves in reverence.
The Sutra on the Unprecedented True Dharma Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Five.
The Sutra on the Unprecedented True Dharma Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Six.
